questions.question: Only one engineer can restore the core payment platform. Which action should the IS auditor recommend to BEST address this workforce risk?

options.A: Cross-train a second engineer and rehearse the restore
options.B: Document the restore steps in a detailed runbook for others
options.C: Buy key-person insurance covering the engineer's absence
options.D: Outsource the platform restore to a managed service vendor

questions.key_concept: Single-person dependency is resolved by building tested capability in another person, not by documents, insurance or outsourcing alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would actually happen on the day the engineer is unavailable. Which option proves someone else can do the restore?
questions.correct_explanation: The risk is that recovery depends on one person. Cross-training a second engineer and rehearsing the restore creates proven, alternate capability, which ISO 22301 expects plans and people to demonstrate through exercises. A runbook is useful, but an untested document read for the first time during an outage often fails; it supports cross-training rather than replacing it.

wrong_explanations.B: A runbook nobody has followed is untested. It helps, but it does not prove anyone else can perform the restore under pressure.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance compensates financially but restores nothing. The platform still cannot be recovered when the engineer is absent.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing moves the dependency to a vendor that does not yet know the platform, and the organization stays accountable for recovery.

tips: Eliminate: C only pays out money, and D shifts the dependency to an outsider who lacks platform knowledge.
Final two: A beats B because a rehearsed second person is tested capability, while a runbook alone is an untested plan.
Exam cue: in continuity questions, tested capability beats untested documentation every time.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the design of a quarterly dashboard for executive oversight of the BCM program. Which metric is MOST useful?

options.A: Number of exercises completed against the annual test plan
options.B: Total program spend compared with the approved budget
options.C: Recovery times achieved in exercises against each RTO
options.D: Maturity score compared with industry peer organizations

questions.key_concept: Executives need outcome metrics: whether recovery capability meets business-set RTOs, not merely whether activities happened or money was spent.
questions.pre_read: Separate metrics that show activity from those that show capability. Which one tells executives the business could actually recover in time?
questions.correct_explanation: Oversight should show whether the program delivers its purpose: recovering critical services within the RTOs the business impact analysis set. Comparing achieved recovery times with RTOs is an outcome measure under ISO 22301 performance evaluation. Counting completed exercises looks rigorous, but it shows activity only; every exercise could run on schedule and still miss its recovery targets.

wrong_explanations.A: Exercise counts and achieved recovery times both come from the test program, yet only one measures outcome; oversight should track results against targets, not activity.
wrong_explanations.B: Spend against budget shows financial control, not whether critical services can be recovered in time.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer maturity scores describe relative process maturity, not whether this organization meets its own recovery objectives.

tips: Eliminate: B tracks money rather than resilience, and D compares process maturity with peers instead of with the firm's own targets.
Final two: C beats A because achieved recovery against RTOs measures outcomes, while exercise counts only measure activity.
Exam cue: for oversight metrics, choose the outcome tied to business objectives over activity or cost counts.

questions.question: Both cloud providers in a firm's failover design are degraded at once, and a third provider holds no production deployment. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Fail over to the third provider using improvised runbooks
options.B: Shift traffic to whichever provider recovers first
options.C: Claim service credits from both providers under their SLAs
options.D: Run in degraded mode with non-critical features disabled

questions.key_concept: When no tested failover path exists, controlled degraded operation protects service more safely than an improvised migration to an untested environment.
questions.pre_read: Note that the third provider has no production deployment. Ask which option keeps customers served without adding untested risk.
questions.correct_explanation: With both planned recovery paths degraded, the safest way to keep critical service running is controlled degraded-mode operation that sheds non-critical features. Failing over to a provider with no production deployment means building and cutting over under pressure with improvised runbooks, an untested change that can corrupt data or cause a second outage. The broken independence assumption should be reviewed after service is stable.

wrong_explanations.A: A third provider would be right if it held a tested deployment. Built in a crisis, it is an untested change; controlled degradation is the safer bet.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting to see which provider recovers leaves customers without a controlled service in the meantime.
wrong_explanations.C: Credits compensate later but keep no service running now.

tips: Eliminate: B waits on the providers' recovery, and C pursues compensation instead of service.
Final two: D beats A because a controlled degraded mode is predictable, while an improvised failover to an empty environment is untested.
Exam cue: in an outage, prefer a known, controlled state over an untested recovery path built on the fly.

questions.question: An online retailer's autoscaling hits a soft service quota in its cloud account, and 28% of requests time out; no queueing exists. What should the IS auditor recommend the operations head do FIRST?

options.A: Raise an urgent quota-increase request with the cloud provider
options.B: Deploy the full site to a secondary region immediately
options.C: Lower the autoscaling trigger so instances launch sooner
options.D: Build request queueing so the site degrades gracefully

questions.key_concept: A soft cloud quota is an administrative limit; asking the provider to lift it is faster and safer than building new controls mid-incident.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of limit was hit and who can lift it fastest.
questions.correct_explanation: The binding constraint is a soft quota, an administrative limit the provider can lift quickly, so an urgent increase request is the fastest way to restore capacity. Building request queueing is sound resilience engineering, but with none in place, designing and deploying it during a live spike is a risky change that will not land sooner than the provider's response.

wrong_explanations.B: A full secondary-region deployment under load is a major, untested change. It takes hours and risks data inconsistency.
wrong_explanations.C: Launching sooner hits the same quota sooner; it adds no capacity beyond the limit.
wrong_explanations.D: Queueing helps future spikes, but building it mid-incident is an untested change that takes longer than lifting a soft quota.

tips: Eliminate: B attempts a risky regional rebuild under load, and C changes when scaling starts, not the limit it hits.
Final two: A beats D because the provider can lift a soft quota quickly, while building queueing mid-incident is slow and risky.
Exam cue: when the limit is administrative, remove it at the source before engineering around it mid-incident.

questions.question: Cloud spend ran at seven times normal for six days because cost-anomaly alerts went only to one engineer on leave. Which recommendation should the IS auditor make to BEST prevent recurrence?

options.A: Lower the anomaly thresholds so overruns are flagged sooner
options.B: Seek a service credit from the provider for the overrun
options.C: Route anomaly alerts to a monitored team queue with backup
options.D: Revoke developers' rights to provision new cloud resources

questions.key_concept: A detective control fails if its alerts reach no one; alert ownership needs a monitored queue and backup, not one individual.
questions.pre_read: Find the exact point where the control broke. Did the alert fail to fire, or did it fire and reach nobody?
questions.correct_explanation: The alerts worked; they reached a single person who was absent, so nobody acted. Routing them to a monitored team queue with a named backup removes that single point of failure in the response. Lowering thresholds is tempting, but it makes alerts fire earlier into the same unattended inbox, so the overrun would still go unnoticed.

wrong_explanations.A: Fix the control where it broke. Lower thresholds would flag spend sooner, a real gain, yet they alert the same absent engineer; delivery and response failed, not detection.
wrong_explanations.B: A credit may recover some cost, but it changes no control and the same gap remains for the next overrun.
wrong_explanations.D: Blocking provisioning halts development work and is disproportionate. It ignores the real failure in alert ownership.

tips: Eliminate: B recovers money without fixing any control, and D blocks legitimate work instead of fixing alert ownership.
Final two: C beats A because the alert fired but reached nobody, so delivery, not sensitivity, must be fixed.
Exam cue: when a control fails, recommend the fix at the exact point it broke.

questions.question: A BIA sets a four-hour RTO for customer support but not the level of service it must provide once resumed. What should the IS auditor recommend the BIA add as MOST important?

options.A: The full normal service level expected within four hours
options.B: The minimum acceptable service level until normal operations return
options.C: The names of staff who will answer calls after recovery
options.D: The recovery strategy and alternate site the process will use

questions.key_concept: Alongside RTO and RPO, the BIA defines the minimum acceptable capacity (MBCO): the reduced service level acceptable until normal operations return.
questions.pre_read: Notice the BIA says when, but not how much. Ask whether support must be fully restored at once.
questions.correct_explanation: An RTO says when a process must resume, but not how much of it. The BIA should also state the minimum acceptable capacity, often called the minimum business continuity objective (MBCO): the reduced service the organization can accept until normal operations return, such as priority calls only. Requiring full normal service within four hours sounds safer, but it inflates recovery cost and ignores that partial service is often acceptable for a time.

wrong_explanations.A: Full service within four hours would be ideal for customers, yet paying for it overstates the need; the BIA records the minimum service the business can accept meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.C: Staff names belong in recovery plans and change often; the BIA defines requirements, not rosters.
wrong_explanations.D: Strategies are chosen after the BIA, from its requirements; the BIA defines what is needed, not how to provide it.

tips: Eliminate: C puts plan rosters in the BIA, and D picks a strategy, which comes after the BIA.
Final two: B beats A because the BIA defines the minimum acceptable service; demanding full service at once overstates the need.
Exam cue: recovery requirements cover how fast (RTO), how much data (RPO) and how much service (minimum acceptable capacity, or MBCO).

questions.subtopic: Shadow AI. Generative AI Use Governance
questions.question: Staff at a consulting firm paste client documents into a free public generative AI tool to draft reports. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Issue an AI acceptable-use rule and provide an approved alternative tool
options.B: Permanently block every generative AI website at the corporate web proxy
options.C: Survey usage and report results to the steering committee
options.D: Ask the tool's provider to delete the uploaded client documents

questions.key_concept: Shadow AI is governed first by an acceptable-use rule for data in AI tools and a sanctioned alternative that meets the business need.
questions.pre_read: Notice why staff use the tool. Ask what happens to that need if the only response is a ban.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff use the tool because it meets a real need, so the first step is governance that covers both sides: a clear rule on what data may go into AI tools, and a sanctioned tool with proper data protections. Blocking public AI sites may help as a stopgap, but on its own, and made permanent, it pushes staff to personal devices, so the leakage continues out of sight.

wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would accept a temporary block as emergency containment, yet a lasting ban leaves the need unmet and the use unseen; govern the tool instead.
wrong_explanations.C: Measuring and reporting usage has value later, but client data keeps leaving while the survey runs.
wrong_explanations.D: A free public tool usually offers no contractual deletion commitment, and asking does not stop further uploads.

tips: Eliminate: C studies the problem while data keeps leaving, and D relies on a provider with no contractual duty.
Final two: A beats B because a rule plus a sanctioned tool meets the need safely; a permanent ban pushes use out of sight.
Exam cue: for shadow IT or shadow AI, pair a clear usage rule with an approved alternative before reaching for blanket bans.

questions.subtopic: Stakeholder Pressure to Skip BCP Exercise
questions.question: Citing acquisition workload, a CFO asks to defer by six months a quarterly failover exercise the bank committed to examiners to verify last quarter's fixes. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the COO?

options.A: Approve the deferral with a signed risk-acceptance memo
options.B: Replace the failover with a walkthrough run by finance staff
options.C: Cancel the exercise and rely on last quarter's results
options.D: Run a failover scoped to the remediated gaps on schedule

questions.key_concept: A regulatory test commitment can be right-sized to resource limits, but it should still be met; scope flexes before the commitment does.
questions.pre_read: Note that the exercise is a commitment to examiners. Ask how to honor it while respecting the real workload pressure.
questions.correct_explanation: The exercise is a commitment to examiners and the way to prove last quarter's gaps were fixed. A scoped failover focused on the remediated gaps keeps that commitment on schedule while easing the load on staff busy with the acquisition. Formal risk acceptance is management's prerogative, but deferring six months breaks a regulatory commitment and leaves recovery capability unproven during a risky integration.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk acceptance is management's right, but a six-month deferral breaks an examiner commitment and leaves remediation unverified during integration.
wrong_explanations.B: A walkthrough by finance staff is a lower-rigor test owned by the wrong team. It cannot prove failover capability.
wrong_explanations.C: Last quarter's exercise found the gaps; it cannot show they are fixed. Relying on it gives false assurance.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps a technical test for a walkthrough by the wrong team, and C relies on results that exposed the gaps.
Final two: D beats A because right-sizing the scope keeps the regulatory commitment, while deferral breaks it.
Exam cue: when a required test clashes with workload, reduce scope before you reduce frequency.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the two job scheduler administrators approve each other's production schedule changes. What should the auditor recommend as the BEST control?

options.A: Log every schedule change and have the administrators review the log
options.B: Rotate scheduler administration duties between the two staff yearly
options.C: Require independent management approval of each production schedule change
options.D: Replace the scheduler with a newer product that has approval workflows

questions.key_concept: Segregation of duties in scheduling separates those who maintain job schedules from those who approve production schedule changes.
questions.pre_read: Notice who approves whose changes. Ask whether anyone outside the pair ever checks a schedule change.
questions.correct_explanation: Two administrators approving each other's changes is mutual self-approval: either can add or alter production jobs, such as payment runs, with a colleague's routine sign-off. Approval by management independent of scheduler administration restores segregation of duties. Logging changes adds a useful trail, but if the same two administrators review it, nobody independent ever examines what they changed, so the weakness remains.

wrong_explanations.A: A change log helps, but review by the same two administrators is still self-review and adds no independence.
wrong_explanations.B: Rotating duties between the same two people changes who acts, not whether anyone independent approves.
wrong_explanations.D: A new tool's workflow is only as independent as the approvers configured in it; the people problem remains.

tips: Eliminate: B rotates the same two people, and D buys a tool without fixing who approves.
Final two: C beats A because independent approval prevents unauthorized changes; a log reviewed by the same administrators is still self-review.
Exam cue: when the people who make changes also approve them, the fix is independent approval, not more logging.

questions.question: Service has been restored after a failed integration cutover whose first rollback attempt also failed. What should the IS auditor recommend management require FIRST before rescheduling the cutover?

options.A: A new cutover date agreed with the integration vendor
options.B: A post-incident review of why the rollback plan failed
options.C: A larger vendor team for the next cutover attempt
options.D: Board re-approval of the original cutover plan unchanged

questions.key_concept: Post-incident reviews identify why changes and rollbacks failed, so lessons shape the next attempt before it is scheduled.
questions.pre_read: Notice that both the cutover and the rollback failed. Ask what must be understood before trying again.
questions.correct_explanation: A post-incident review finds why the cutover and its rollback both failed, so the next plan, including a tested rollback, is built on those lessons. A new date with the vendor feels like progress, but rescheduling before understanding the failure invites the same outcome, this time with the business already knowing the fallback does not work.

wrong_explanations.A: Rescheduling is a necessary next step, yet a date set before the review invites a repeat; lessons must shape the plan before the calendar does.
wrong_explanations.C: More staff does not fix a flawed plan or an untested rollback.
wrong_explanations.D: Re-approving the failed approach ignores the evidence that it did not work.

tips: Eliminate: C adds people to a flawed plan, and D re-approves what already failed.
Final two: B beats A because lessons learned must shape the next plan before any date is set.
Exam cue: after a failed change or recovery, review why it failed before trying again.

questions.question: Twelve production batch jobs run under the personal account of an administrator who left last month; the account stays active so the jobs do not fail. Which recommendation from the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Move the jobs to owned service accounts; disable the leaver's account
options.B: Reset the account's password and give it to the operations manager
options.C: Keep the account active and review its activity each month
options.D: Delete the jobs from the scheduler until a new owner is found

questions.key_concept: Scheduled production jobs run under owned service accounts, not personal ones, so leavers can be removed without breaking processing.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the account was kept active. Ask which option removes the leaver's access without stopping the jobs.
questions.correct_explanation: Jobs tied to a person's account break or stay exposed whenever that person leaves. Moving them, through change management, to dedicated service accounts with a named owner and restricted rights lets the leaver's account be disabled without stopping production. Resetting the password removes the leaver's access, but the jobs still depend on a personal identity, now shared, so actions are no longer traceable to one person.

wrong_explanations.B: This cuts off the leaver, but a shared personal login loses accountability, and the jobs still depend on one person's account.
wrong_explanations.C: A monthly review only detects misuse after it happens; the leaver's access stays live throughout.
wrong_explanations.D: Removing the jobs stops production processing, trading a security gap for an availability failure.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a leaver's access live and only watches it, and D stops production processing to fix an account issue.
Final two: A beats B because service accounts remove the personal dependency; a reset password just shares one person's identity.
Exam cue: people get named personal accounts; automated jobs get owned service accounts. Either way, every account has one accountable owner.

questions.question: At hour 18 of a 24-hour DR exercise, only 30% of recovery objectives are met, and the FDIC will receive the report. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the business continuity head?

options.A: Stop the test now to limit staff overtime costs
options.B: Restart from hour zero and report the rerun results instead
options.C: Finish the test and brief the examiner on ranked failures
options.D: Close the exercise record with an internal lessons-learned memo

questions.key_concept: A failed exercise is valuable evidence: finish it as planned, analyze the failures for remediation and be transparent with the regulator.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the exercise is for. Does a failure need hiding or improving, or does it need analyzing and reporting honestly?
questions.correct_explanation: An exercise exists to find weaknesses, and this one has found several. Finishing it within the planned window gathers evidence on the remaining steps, ranking failures by cause drives remediation, and briefing the examiner early preserves regulatory trust. An internal lessons-learned memo records the failures, but it neither drives prioritized remediation nor prepares the regulator, who will read the report anyway.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping early saves hours but loses evidence on the remaining recovery steps the regulator expects.
wrong_explanations.B: Reporting a clean rerun instead of the actual result misleads the regulator and hides the failures the exercise exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: A memo documents the failures but lacks prioritized remediation and leaves the examiner to discover the problems unprepared.

tips: Eliminate: A gives up the remaining evidence to save cost, and B replaces the actual result with a rerun.
Final two: C beats D because analyzed failures and proactive regulator contact drive remediation, while a memo only records.
Exam cue: when a regulator will read a failed test, finish it, rank the failures and brief the examiner early; never swap in a rerun.

questions.subtopic: Data Corruption Recovery vs Business Deadline
questions.question: Storage corruption has damaged 8% of yesterday's trade records on settlement day; restoring the clean backup and replaying logs takes 6–8 hours, well before the cutoff. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Settle using best-available data and correct the records afterward
options.B: Reconcile each affected trade manually before settling
options.C: Ask the clearing firm for an extension before taking action
options.D: Restore the clean backup and replay the logs

questions.key_concept: When one recovery path yields complete, verified data before the deadline, recommend it; only when every path costs data or time does management choose.
questions.pre_read: Compare the recovery options against the deadline. Which one produces complete, verified data in time?
questions.correct_explanation: Settlement must rest on accurate records. Restoring the clean backup and replaying the transaction logs is the fastest route to verified data. Manual reconciliation is accurate in principle, but reworking thousands of trades by hand is far slower and more error-prone than a replay. The replay loses no committed trades and finishes in time, so there is no trade-off for management to weigh.

wrong_explanations.A: Settling on known-corrupt data harms customers and breaches books-and-records duties. Later correction does not undo that.
wrong_explanations.B: Manual reconciliation is a valid control when no clean source exists, but here a clean backup and log replay delivers verified data faster and without hand-keying errors.
wrong_explanations.C: Extensions are rarely granted, and waiting for an answer wastes hours that the restore needs.

tips: Eliminate: A knowingly settles on corrupt data, and C spends scarce hours waiting for an unlikely extension.
Final two: D beats B because a backup replay yields verified data far faster and more reliably than manual rework.
Exam cue: when one recovery path gives complete, verified data in time, recommend it; when every path costs data or time, management chooses.

questions.subtopic: Help Desk Overwhelmed During Major Event
questions.question: During a campus email outage, help-desk tickets jump fivefold, mostly duplicates from users unaware the outage is universal. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Reassign administrative staff to answer help-desk phone queues
options.B: Broadcast an outage notice with scheduled status updates
options.C: Contract a commercial call center for surge capacity
options.D: Redirect the help-desk line to the email vendor's support

questions.key_concept: When demand is driven by duplicate reports of a known incident, communication cuts demand faster than adding service desk capacity.
questions.pre_read: Look at why tickets are rising. Ask whether the problem is too few agents or too many avoidable contacts.
questions.correct_explanation: Most tickets are duplicates from users who do not know the outage is already known. A broadcast notice with scheduled status updates removes the reason to call, cutting demand at the source, as ITIL major-incident communication intends. Reassigning staff adds capacity, but untrained agents still answer the same avoidable calls, and queues stay long while users keep contacting the desk.

wrong_explanations.A: Extra untrained staff add some capacity but leave the cause, users not knowing, untouched, so avoidable contacts keep coming.
wrong_explanations.C: Onboarding a call center takes time and its agents lack local context. It also treats volume rather than its cause.
wrong_explanations.D: The institution keeps ownership of its users' incidents. Sending them to a vendor line abandons them and confuses the response.

tips: Eliminate: C is slow to onboard and lacks context, and D sends the institution's own users to a vendor that does not own the incident.
Final two: B beats A because clear communication removes avoidable contacts, while extra staff only absorbs them.
Exam cue: when volume comes from duplicate reports, reduce demand with communication before adding capacity.

questions.question: A key SaaS customer's acquisitions will raise its API traffic 3.4 times within four weeks, beyond current capacity. What should the IS auditor recommend the CTO do FIRST?

options.A: Model the projected load and agree a phased onboarding plan
options.B: Accept the volume and accelerate scaling to meet the date
options.C: Refuse the extra volume under the existing contract terms
options.D: Negotiate a volume premium at the next contract renewal

questions.key_concept: Capacity management models demand before committing; phasing new load protects every tenant's service while capacity is proven.
questions.pre_read: Notice the four-week deadline and the size of the jump. Ask what must be known before promising anything.
questions.correct_explanation: Capacity management starts by modeling the projected demand against current limits, then shaping how it arrives. A phased onboarding plan lets capacity be added and proven step by step without degrading other customers. Accepting the full volume and racing to scale meets the customer's date, but it commits to untested capacity and puts every tenant's service at risk if scaling falls short.

wrong_explanations.B: Scaling to the date would honor a key customer's timeline, yet committing before modeling stakes all tenants on capacity nobody has proven; model demand first.
wrong_explanations.C: Refusing a key customer's growth damages the relationship and revenue without exploring a safe way to support it.
wrong_explanations.D: Pricing at the next renewal ignores the four-week capacity problem; the load arrives long before the contract changes.

tips: Eliminate: C turns away a key customer, and D addresses price months after the load arrives.
Final two: A beats B because modeled, phased onboarding protects all tenants, while an untested scale-up risks everyone's service.
Exam cue: in capacity questions, model the demand first, then commit to a plan you can prove.

questions.question: A cloud vendor has missed its 99.95% SLA for 90 days despite an agreed remediation roadmap; credits cover about 8% of business impact. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the CTO?

options.A: Measure SLA performance against the remediation plan for another quarter
options.B: Migrate production to an alternative cloud vendor right away
options.C: Issue a formal cure notice with escalating penalties for further misses
options.D: Build resilience to vendor failures and plan an exit

questions.key_concept: SLA credits do not transfer business impact; the organization stays accountable for resilience and must design critical services around vendor failures.
questions.pre_read: Compare the credits with the business impact. Ask who really bears the cost when the vendor falls short.
questions.correct_explanation: Credits cover a small fraction of the impact, which shows the firm, not the vendor, carries the risk. The firm remains accountable for its service, so the lasting fix is to design critical services to tolerate vendor degradation and to prepare an exit plan. A cure notice is a legitimate contractual step, but the vendor has already agreed a remediation roadmap and the pattern continues; more contract pressure changes little for customers.

wrong_explanations.A: The roadmap has already failed for 90 days. Another quarter of measurement leaves the business absorbing losses that credits barely cover.
wrong_explanations.B: An immediate migration is a large, risky change, and a new vendor can also degrade without resilient design.
wrong_explanations.C: Penalties add contract pressure, but an agreed roadmap has already failed for 90 days, and credits or penalties do not protect customers.

tips: Eliminate: A waits another quarter on a failing roadmap, and B makes a rushed, risky move that does not remove vendor dependence.
Final two: D beats C because credits cover only 8% of the impact; the firm must own resilience and an exit path, not apply more contract pressure.
Exam cue: SLA credits are not a risk response; when a vendor keeps failing, build resilience you control.

questions.question: A BIA sets recovery time objectives for each process but does not record the staff, skills and equipment needed to resume them. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Shorten the recovery time objectives to add a safety margin
options.B: Let each department estimate its resources during an actual disruption
options.C: Extend the BIA to capture minimum resources for recovery
options.D: Buy spare equipment for each department in advance

questions.key_concept: The BIA should record the minimum resources (people, skills, equipment, records, systems) each critical process needs to resume.
questions.pre_read: Notice the BIA records time but not resources. Ask what a recovery strategy needs besides a deadline.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery time objectives say how fast a process must resume; strategies also need to know what it takes, such as minimum staff, key skills, equipment, records and systems. Recording these in the BIA lets strategies and plans be sized correctly. Buying spare equipment in advance looks proactive, but without known requirements it may buy the wrong items and still ignores people and skills.

wrong_explanations.A: Tighter targets without known resource needs make plans harder to meet, not more realistic.
wrong_explanations.B: Estimating during a disruption wastes time when recovery should already be under way.
wrong_explanations.D: Requirements come before procurement. Pre-positioned equipment is a recognized strategy, yet bought blind it may be the wrong kit, and people and skills stay unplanned.

tips: Eliminate: A tightens targets without the facts, and B waits for a crisis to plan.
Final two: C beats D because recorded requirements size the strategy; buying ahead without them is guesswork.
Exam cue: a complete BIA records what each critical process needs to recover, not only how quickly.

questions.question: A remediation action to test the incident response plan, untested for 2.5 years, was closed after only a document revision. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Accept the closure because the plan document was revised
options.B: Reopen the action until a plan test evidences remediation
options.C: Close the finding since no major incident occurred this year
options.D: Obtain a signed attestation from the incident response lead

questions.key_concept: Remediation actions close only on evidence the control operates; for response plans, that evidence is a documented test.
questions.pre_read: Notice the item was closed without a test. Ask what proof would show a response plan actually works.
questions.correct_explanation: Remediation closes on evidence that the control now operates, and for a response plan that evidence is a test, such as a tabletop or simulation, with results and fixes recorded. Reopening the action keeps it tracked until that proof exists. A signed attestation looks formal, but it is the owner's own assertion, not evidence that the plan would work.

wrong_explanations.A: A revised document shows the plan was edited, not that it works; untested plans often fail on contacts, roles and tooling.
wrong_explanations.C: A quiet year says nothing about readiness; the plan exists for the incident that has not happened yet.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor may use an attestation to confirm accountability for the action, yet closure needs evidence the control operates; for a response plan, that means a test.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an edited document as proof, and C treats a quiet year as evidence of readiness.
Final two: B beats D because closure needs test evidence that the plan works; an attestation is only the owner's assertion.
Exam cue: a remediation action closes on evidence the control operates, not on management's word.

questions.subtopic: Log Management. Personal Data in Logs
questions.question: An IS auditor finds application debug logs record full customer names, card numbers and addresses in plain text. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Encrypt the log storage so the files are protected at rest
options.B: Shorten retention for the debug logs to seven days
options.C: Restrict log access to the operations and security teams
options.D: Mask or remove personal data before events are logged

questions.key_concept: Log content should be minimized: mask or exclude personal and card data at the source, then protect what logs must keep.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the debug logs contain. Ask whether operations ever needs that data in a log.
questions.correct_explanation: Logs should capture what operations and security need, not full personal and card data. Masking or removing that data at the source applies data minimization, so it never spreads into log platforms, backups and support tools. Encrypting log storage protects files at rest, but anyone able to read the logs still sees full card numbers, and copies made from them carry the data onward.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption at rest protects stored files, not data viewed by log users or copied into other tools.
wrong_explanations.B: Shorter retention reduces the window but still writes full card and personal data every day.
wrong_explanations.C: Access restriction narrows who sees the data but leaves it collected without need.

tips: Eliminate: B and C shrink exposure but keep collecting data that should never be logged.
Final two: D beats A because minimizing at the source removes the data; encryption still lets every log reader see it.
Exam cue: when logs hold sensitive data, minimize at the source before protecting what remains.

questions.question: A firm's disaster recovery tests restore every application server, but its Active Directory domain controllers are left out of every test. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Rebuild a domain controller from backup in an isolated environment
options.B: Rely on the domain controllers replicating to the recovery site
options.C: Back up the domain controllers more often than at present
options.D: Have the backup vendor certify its software supports directories

questions.key_concept: Directory services underpin every recovered system, so their restore from backup must be tested; replication is not a backup.
questions.pre_read: Ask what every restored application needs before users can log in, and what replication would copy along with the data.
questions.correct_explanation: Every application restored in a test still needs the directory to authenticate users and services, so an untested directory restore puts the whole recovery at risk. An isolated restore proves the backups work without touching production. Replication to the recovery site gives availability, but it copies corruption, mass deletions or an attacker's changes to every controller at once; only a known-good backup recovers from those.

wrong_explanations.B: Replication keeps a live copy but also spreads corruption or malicious changes, so it cannot replace a tested restore from backup.
wrong_explanations.C: More frequent backups do not show that any of them can be restored; the gap is the missing test.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor's certification describes the product, not whether this firm's directory backups restore in its environment.

tips: Eliminate: C adds backups without proving any restore, and D relies on a vendor claim instead of a test.
Final two: A beats B because replication copies damage to every controller; only a tested restore from backup proves recovery.
Exam cue: shared services such as the directory come first in recovery, so their restore must be proven, not assumed.

questions.question: An actively exploited flaw appears in an open-source library used by 340 services, and each safe rollout takes 4–6 hours. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Patch services in the standard change-board priority order
options.B: Patch internal microservices first, then customer-facing APIs
options.C: Patch exposed services first, shielded by interim WAF rules
options.D: Hand the rollout prioritization to an external IR firm

questions.key_concept: When patching cannot be instant, prioritize by exposure and use compensating controls to cover the window until each service is patched.
questions.pre_read: Note the rollout time per service. Ask which services attackers can reach first and how to protect them meanwhile.
questions.correct_explanation: With hundreds of services and hours per rollout, exposure decides the order: internet-facing services are reachable first, so they are patched first, while interim WAF rules shield them until the fix lands. This applies risk-based patch management under emergency change. The standard change-board order keeps governance, but routine priorities ignore which services an active exploit can reach today.

wrong_explanations.A: Change control still applies, but a routine priority order ignores exposure while attackers exploit reachable services.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal services are harder to reach. Patching them first leaves the most exposed, customer-facing surface open longest.
wrong_explanations.D: External responders can help, but prioritizing the firm's own services is a management decision it cannot hand off.

tips: Eliminate: B patches the least exposed services first, and D hands away a decision management owns.
Final two: C beats A because an active exploit demands exposure-based emergency priorities, not the routine change order.
Exam cue: when everything cannot be patched at once, patch by exposure and add a compensating control meanwhile.

questions.question: Eleven tenants on a shared SaaS platform report SLA breaches because one newly signed tenant runs six times the average workload. What should the IS auditor recommend the CTO do FIRST?

options.A: Add shared capacity until the large tenant's load is absorbed
options.B: Enforce per-tenant resource quotas sized to each contract
options.C: Renegotiate the large tenant's contract to add volume pricing
options.D: Measure each tenant's load for a month, then review quotas

questions.key_concept: Multi-tenant service levels depend on isolation; per-tenant quotas stop one workload from consuming capacity contracted to others.
questions.pre_read: Ask why one tenant can hurt eleven others. Which option removes that ability rather than paying for its effects?
questions.correct_explanation: The breaches occur because nothing stops one tenant from consuming capacity sold to others. Per-tenant quotas sized to each contract restore isolation, so every customer gets what it pays for. Adding shared capacity eases pressure for now, but without isolation the large tenant's growth will absorb the new headroom and the breaches will return.

wrong_explanations.A: Added capacity does relieve the other tenants at once, yet one unconstrained tenant will consume it; fix the cause, not the symptom.
wrong_explanations.C: Pricing changes take time and do not stop the workload from degrading other tenants today.
wrong_explanations.D: The cause is already known. A month of measurement leaves eleven tenants in breach while isolation could be enforced now.

tips: Eliminate: C changes price without changing the load, and D delays a month although the cause is already known.
Final two: B beats A because isolation fixes the cause, while added shared capacity is absorbed by the same tenant.
Exam cue: in shared environments, fix isolation before adding capacity.

questions.subtopic: Data Backup. Electronic Vaulting and RPO Fit
questions.question: A BIA sets a one-hour RPO for a firm's order database. Which copy method, if relied on, should MOST concern the IS auditor?

options.A: Remote journaling of each committed transaction to the recovery site
options.B: Asynchronous replication of the database to the recovery site
options.C: Electronic vaulting of backup batches every 30 minutes
options.D: Hourly database snapshots copied to the recovery site each night

questions.key_concept: A copy method's data-loss window is the gap between copies; it must be shorter than the RPO set by the BIA.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask how often data actually leaves the site, then compare that gap with the one-hour RPO.
questions.correct_explanation: Snapshots taken hourly but copied offsite only nightly can lose up to a day of orders if the primary site is lost, far beyond the one-hour RPO. Electronic vaulting every 30 minutes is the slowest network method and looks like the weak link, but its worst case of about half an hour stays within the objective.

wrong_explanations.A: Journaling sends each transaction as it happens, so loss is limited to the last few moments; it meets a one-hour RPO easily.
wrong_explanations.B: Asynchronous replication copies writes moments after they commit, so the possible loss is seconds or minutes, well within an hour.
wrong_explanations.C: Batches leave the site every 30 minutes, capping the loss at about half an hour, so this method still meets the one-hour objective.

tips: Eliminate: A and B send data continuously or within moments, so both clearly meet the one-hour objective.
Final two: D beats C because snapshots that leave the site only nightly can lose a day of orders; 30-minute vaulting is slower than replication but stays inside the hour.
Exam cue: know each copy method's loss window: journaling and replication lose seconds, vaulting one batch interval, anything sent offsite nightly up to a day.

questions.subtopic: Litigation Hold During Active BCP Exercise
questions.question: During a planned DR exercise, legal counsel issues a litigation hold covering data on systems the exercise will overwrite from backup. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Finish the exercise, then forensically image the affected systems afterward
options.B: Terminate the exercise and reschedule it once the hold is lifted
options.C: Pause the overwriting steps until counsel confirms the hold's scope
options.D: Continue the exercise and record the hold in the test log

questions.key_concept: A litigation hold overrides routine operations: pause the steps that would destroy covered data, and let counsel set the scope.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the restore would overwrite covered data. Ask which option stops the harm without abandoning the recovery test entirely.
questions.correct_explanation: A litigation hold is a legal duty to preserve data, and a restore from backup would destroy the very state the hold protects. Pausing only the overwriting steps preserves evidence while counsel defines scope, and unaffected parts of the test can resume. Terminating until the hold lifts also preserves data, but holds can last years, leaving the recovery plan untested far too long.

wrong_explanations.A: Imaging afterward is too late: the restore will already have overwritten the production state the hold requires the firm to preserve.
wrong_explanations.B: This preserves data but over-corrects. Holds can run for years, and the firm would be left with an untested recovery plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Logging the hold does nothing to stop the restore from destroying data that must be preserved, exposing the firm to spoliation claims.

tips: Eliminate: A preserves data only after it is overwritten, and D documents the hold without protecting anything.
Final two: C beats B because a targeted pause meets the legal duty without leaving the recovery plan untested for an open-ended period.
Exam cue: when a legal preservation duty collides with an operation, stop only the conflicting steps and let counsel define scope.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that customer records can be deleted while open orders still point to them, leaving orphan orders. Which database control is MOST LIKELY missing?

options.A: Entity integrity requiring a unique key for each customer
options.B: Referential integrity enforced between the two tables
options.C: Record locking during simultaneous updates to customer data
options.D: Nightly backups of the customer and order tables

questions.key_concept: Referential integrity makes every foreign key match an existing primary key, so linked records cannot be orphaned by deletes.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether the fault is inside one table or in the link between two tables, then pick the matching rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Referential integrity requires every foreign key, such as the customer number on an order, to match an existing primary key. Enforced in the database, it blocks deleting a customer who still has open orders, so orphans cannot arise. Entity integrity sounds close, but it only makes each customer's own key unique and non-empty; it says nothing about records in other tables that point to it.

wrong_explanations.A: Entity integrity sounds close because it protects customer keys, but it only keeps each row's own key unique and present; it cannot stop deleting a customer that orders still reference.
wrong_explanations.C: Locking prevents two users overwriting each other's changes at the same moment. It does not check links between tables.
wrong_explanations.D: Backups help recover lost data but do not stop the deletion that creates orphan orders.

tips: Eliminate: C handles simultaneous updates and D recovers data after the fact; neither checks links between tables.
Final two: B beats A because the fault is a broken link between tables; entity integrity covers only a table's own keys.
Exam cue: MOST LIKELY asks for the best-fitting cause; match the symptom, here a broken link between tables, to the control that governs it.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the DR design replicates customer data nightly to a region where a data-localization law forbids storing any copy. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Suspend replication and accept the loss of DR coverage
options.B: Rely on the provider's contract for transfer compliance
options.C: Encrypt the replicated data in transit and at rest with customer-held keys
options.D: Move DR to a compliant region that still meets RTO and RPO

questions.key_concept: DR site selection must satisfy data residency rules and recovery objectives together; encryption does not change where data resides.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is prohibited: the location, not the exposure. Ask which option fixes the location without losing recovery capability.
questions.correct_explanation: Relocating the DR target to a compliant region removes the prohibited copies while keeping recovery capability, provided the new site is tested against the agreed RTO and RPO. Encryption with customer-held keys is a strong safeguard, but it does not change where the copies reside; a localization law that forbids storing data in a region applies however well the data is protected.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping replication ends the transfer but leaves critical systems with no recovery path, trading a compliance breach for an unacceptable continuity gap.
wrong_explanations.B: A contract cannot override a localization law, and the organization stays accountable for where its customer data is stored.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption protects confidentiality, but the replicated copies still sit in a region where the localization law forbids storing them.

tips: Eliminate: A removes recovery capability to solve a location problem, and B leans on a contract that cannot override the law.
Final two: D beats C because the location itself is prohibited; encryption protects the copies but they still reside there.
Exam cue: when a DR design breaks a constraint, redesign the site and re-prove RTO and RPO rather than dropping recovery.

questions.subtopic: IoT Device Fleet Compromised in Field
questions.question: Threat hunters at a sensor manufacturer find 14,000 field IoT sensors beaconing to attacker infrastructure, and the firmware-update credentials were leaked publicly. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Block the command channel and revoke the leaked update credentials
options.B: Push an over-the-air firmware update to every deployed field sensor
options.C: Recall and physically replace each sensor at customer sites
options.D: Ask affected customers to remediate the sensors on their networks

questions.key_concept: Contain first: cut attacker command and control and revoke leaked credentials before remediating through any channel they could abuse.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the update credentials are public. Ask whether the remediation channel can be trusted yet.
questions.correct_explanation: Containment comes first: cutting the command channel stops the attacker steering compromised sensors, and revoking the leaked credentials closes the path used to tamper with firmware. A fleet-wide update is the right remediation later, but pushing it while the update credentials are still exposed risks the attacker using, or racing, that same channel.

wrong_explanations.B: A fleet update will be the eventual fix, yet pushed while its credentials are public it shares the channel with the attacker; contain first, then remediate.
wrong_explanations.C: Replacing a whole fleet takes months and costs far more than needed, while compromised sensors stay under attacker control in the meantime.
wrong_explanations.D: The manufacturer owns the firmware and the leak. Pushing remediation onto customers leaves the root cause untouched and response uneven.

tips: Eliminate: C is a slow, disproportionate recall, and D hands the manufacturer's problem to customers.
Final two: A beats B because the update channel itself is compromised; contain and revoke access before remediating through it.
Exam cue: in an active compromise, cut attacker control and revoke stolen credentials before rolling out fixes.

questions.question: A validated BIA has gone no further than the continuity team, and IT is now selecting recovery strategies from it. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Let IT finalize strategies and seek budget approval later
options.B: Obtain senior management approval of the BIA results and priorities
options.C: Repeat the BIA using an external continuity consultant
options.D: Have the business continuity manager sign off the BIA instead

questions.key_concept: Senior management approves BIA results, confirming recovery priorities and the basis for funding continuity strategies.
questions.pre_read: Notice who has and has not accepted the BIA. Ask who decides priorities and spending.
questions.correct_explanation: BIA results set recovery priorities and drive spending, so senior management must review and approve them before strategies are chosen. Approval confirms the priorities reflect the organization's risk appetite and commits funding. Sign-off by the business continuity manager records completion, but the manager facilitated the analysis and cannot accept enterprise risk or commit budgets on management's behalf.

wrong_explanations.C: Redoing the analysis is wasteful when the gap is approval, not the work itself.
wrong_explanations.D: The continuity manager facilitates the BIA but cannot accept enterprise risk or commit funding.

tips: Eliminate: A spends before priorities are agreed, and C redoes work that only lacks approval.
Final two: B beats D because senior management owns risk and funding; the facilitator's sign-off can commit neither.

questions.question: A new production credit-scoring model version approves applicants from certain neighborhoods at markedly lower rates than the validated, deployable prior version. Which action would the IS auditor consider MOST appropriate for management to take FIRST?

options.A: Roll back to the prior validated version under emergency change
options.B: Keep the new version live and add a fairness dashboard
options.C: Drop the location field and push a hotfix release today
options.D: Route decisions to human review while the release is investigated

questions.key_concept: When a release causes harm and a validated prior version exists, back out the release through emergency change before investigating root cause.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problem began with the new release. Ask whether a known-good state exists and how fast it can be restored.
questions.correct_explanation: The harmful behavior arrived with the new release and a validated prior version exists, so restoring it through emergency change removes the cause quickly and keeps an approval record. Root cause can then be found offline. Human review also contains decisions, but it is a workaround: the faulty release stays live, and reviewers must spot a subtle pattern across high volumes.

wrong_explanations.B: A dashboard measures the disparity but leaves the faulty release making the same skewed decisions for every new applicant.
wrong_explanations.C: Proxy features can carry the pattern without the field, and a same-day hotfix adds a second unvalidated change to production.
wrong_explanations.D: Human review shares the rollback's aim of stopping unfair decisions, yet the faulty model keeps scoring; with a validated version available, remove the cause.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the faulty release deciding, and C pushes an untested hotfix that proxy features may defeat.
Final two: A beats D because restoring the known-good version removes the cause, while human review only works around it.
Exam cue: when a new release causes harm and a validated prior version exists, back it out first, then investigate.

questions.subtopic: Tax Authority IT Audit During Planned Outage
questions.question: A weekend database upgrade carries a patch for an actively exploited flaw, but tax auditors request uninterrupted system access starting during that window. What should the IS auditor recommend to the CFO FIRST?

options.A: Run the upgrade and give the tax auditors data extracts afterward
options.B: Defer the upgrade and accept the exploit risk until the audit ends
options.C: Ask the tax authority to start its fieldwork after the upgrade
options.D: Isolate the database from the network until the audit ends

questions.key_concept: When a security patch and a regulator's request clash on timing, negotiate the sequence before accepting risk on either side.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the conflict is about timing, not substance. Ask whether one short delay could satisfy both parties.
questions.correct_explanation: Both obligations can usually be met by sequencing them. Asking the tax authority to start once the short upgrade window closes keeps the exploited flaw on track to be patched and gives the auditors full access soon after. Deferring the upgrade also avoids conflict, but it leaves an actively exploited vulnerability open for days to solve a timing issue a conversation may fix.

wrong_explanations.A: Extracts after the fact do not give the uninterrupted live access the authority requested.
wrong_explanations.B: Seek to meet both duties before trading one away. Deferral is a valid risk response, yet it leaves an exploited flaw open over a timing clash.
wrong_explanations.D: Isolation blocks the auditors' access too, and leaves the exploited flaw unpatched.

tips: Eliminate: A replaces the requested live access with later extracts, and D cuts off the auditors while leaving the flaw unpatched.
Final two: C beats B because agreeing on sequence protects both the patch and the audit, while deferral accepts exploit risk first.
Exam cue: when two legitimate obligations clash on timing, try sequencing by agreement before sacrificing either one.

questions.question: A trigger bug silently corrupted 0.3% of invoices over 90 days, and backups older than 30 days have rotated out. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Notify every customer that past invoices may be inaccurate
options.B: Restore the latest backup and replay valid transactions
options.C: Fix the trigger and leave historical invoices as issued
options.D: Query the invoice data to identify every affected record

questions.key_concept: With no clean backup, analyze the data to identify and quantify the corruption before correcting records or notifying customers.
questions.pre_read: Compare the 90-day corruption with the 30-day backup retention. Ask whether any clean copy exists at all.
questions.correct_explanation: No clean backup exists, because every retained copy already contains corruption. The firm must therefore analyze the data to find which invoices are wrong and by how much. That scope drives correction, customer remediation, disclosure and financial reporting. Notifying every customer first is a transparent instinct, but without knowing who is affected it alarms the 99.7% with correct invoices.

wrong_explanations.A: Blanket notice before scoping alarms customers whose invoices are correct and gives affected customers no useful detail on the error.
wrong_explanations.B: Retained backups postdate the start of corruption, so restoring one brings back bad data and discards valid later work.
wrong_explanations.C: Fixing the cause is needed, but leaving known-wrong invoices in place keeps billing and financial records inaccurate.

tips: Eliminate: B overlooks that no clean backup exists, and C leaves known-wrong records uncorrected.
Final two: D beats A because you must know which records are wrong before telling customers anything useful.
Exam cue: when data integrity fails and no clean copy exists, scope the damage before remediating or notifying.

questions.subtopic: Log Retention. Preservation for Regulator Request
questions.question: A data protection authority requests 18 months of transfer logs, but the log platform keeps 90 days online and overwrites older archives monthly. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Answer using the 90 days of logs currently held online
options.B: Suspend archive rotation so requested logs are not overwritten
options.C: Ask counsel to seek an extension while the logs are rebuilt
options.D: Extend the log retention policy to 18 months for future requests

questions.key_concept: When logs are requested for an inquiry, preserve them by suspending scheduled deletion before retrieval or retention policy changes.
questions.pre_read: Notice the archives are overwritten monthly. Ask what will be lost if nothing changes today.
questions.correct_explanation: Monthly rotation is destroying records the authority has asked for, so preservation comes first; retrieval and review can follow once nothing more is lost. Extending retention to 18 months is a sound control fix, but it governs future logs only and does nothing to stop this month's rotation overwriting the archives already requested.

wrong_explanations.A: Ninety days covers a fraction of the requested period, and the older archives keep being overwritten while the reply is prepared.
wrong_explanations.C: Overwritten logs cannot be rebuilt, and extra time does nothing to stop the rotation that is destroying the requested records.
wrong_explanations.D: A longer policy fixes future retention but does not stop this month's rotation overwriting the logs already requested.

tips: Eliminate: A answers with a fraction of the period, and C seeks time while rotation keeps destroying records.
Final two: B beats D because the requested logs must be preserved now; a new policy only protects future records.
Exam cue: when records are requested, stop scheduled deletion first, then fix the retention policy.

questions.subtopic: SOC for Cybersecurity Report Audit Reliance
questions.question: The CISO presents a managed security provider's SOC for Cybersecurity report to the audit committee as evidence of the firm's own program. What is the BEST response from the IS auditor?

options.A: Accept it because the service auditor's opinion is unmodified
options.B: Defer to the CISO's judgment on the report's sufficiency
options.C: Accept it once the complementary user entity controls are confirmed
options.D: Use it for provider reliance and test the firm's controls

questions.key_concept: A service provider's report covers the provider's controls; the firm's own program still needs separate audit evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose controls the report actually covers. Then ask what the audit committee believes it covers.
questions.correct_explanation: The report covers the provider's cybersecurity program, not the firm's. It supports reliance on the provider, but the firm's own program needs separate evidence. Confirming complementary user entity controls is a good reliance step, yet those controls cover only the firm's side of the outsourced service, not its whole cybersecurity program.

wrong_explanations.A: An unmodified opinion speaks only to the provider's subject matter. It says nothing about controls the firm itself operates.
wrong_explanations.B: The auditor must reach an independent conclusion on evidence sufficiency; deferring to the program owner impairs objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: User entity controls cover the firm's side of the outsourced service only, leaving the rest of the firm's program untested.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses a clean opinion with relevant scope, and B surrenders the auditor's independent judgment.
Final two: D beats C because user entity controls complete reliance on one service, not assurance over the whole program.
Exam cue: before relying on any third-party report, check whose controls it covers and whether that matches your audit objective.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds administrators often lower server logging levels while troubleshooting, without approval or record, and seldom restore them. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Remind administrators of the logging policy in annual training
options.B: Review the logging settings of each server once a year
options.C: Put logging changes under change control and alert on them
options.D: Remove administrators' access to the servers they support

questions.key_concept: Logging configuration is a controlled setting; changes need approval and alerts, so reduced logging is noticed and restored rather than left in place.
questions.pre_read: Notice logging is lowered and seldom restored. Ask how anyone would know a server was logging less.
questions.correct_explanation: Lowering logging during troubleshooting may be needed, but unapproved, unrecorded changes that are seldom reversed leave servers logging less with nobody aware of the gap. Treating logging configuration as a controlled change, with approval, and alerting when settings change, makes every reduction visible so it can be restored promptly. An annual review of settings would eventually reveal reduced logging, but events during the months before would go unrecorded.

wrong_explanations.A: Training explains the rule but does nothing to detect or reverse a change to logging.
wrong_explanations.B: A yearly configuration review is a standard detective check, yet unapproved logging cuts happen often and lose events at once; each change must surface when it happens.
wrong_explanations.D: Administrators need access to troubleshoot servers; removing it stops operations rather than controlling logging.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats a policy administrators already know and bypass, and D blocks the work administrators must do.
Final two: C beats B because change control and alerts expose reduced logging quickly; an annual review leaves months unrecorded.
Exam cue: treat logging settings as controlled configuration; changes need approval and an alert so gaps are seen and closed.

questions.question: A firm moves to terminate its failing claims-processing vendor, which invokes an 18-month exit clause and a large penalty. What is the BEST recommendation from the IS auditor to the COO?

options.A: Secure transition services while counsel tests the breach claim
options.B: Pay the penalty and cut over to a new platform immediately
options.C: Sue for breach and withhold payments during the litigation
options.D: Accept the 18-month exit term and plan the full migration within it

questions.key_concept: In a contested vendor exit, protect continuity of the critical service while pursuing contractual remedies in parallel.
questions.pre_read: Notice that claims processing cannot stop. Ask which option keeps service running without giving up the firm's rights.
questions.correct_explanation: Claims processing cannot stop, so continuity must be secured through a transition services arrangement while counsel tests whether the repeated failures amount to material breach, which may void the penalty. Accepting the 18-month term keeps service running, but it waives the firm's strongest legal position and leaves it tied to a distressed, insecure vendor.

wrong_explanations.B: Paying immediately gives up the breach argument, and cutting over without migration and testing risks a gap in a critical service.
wrong_explanations.C: Withholding payment from the only processor of claims invites service suspension and puts continuity at risk during litigation.
wrong_explanations.D: This keeps service running but concedes the penalty and keeps a failing, breached vendor in place for 18 months.

tips: Eliminate: B cuts over without a tested migration, and C provokes a service stoppage mid-dispute.
Final two: A beats D because it protects continuity without conceding the firm's legal position against a failing vendor.
Exam cue: in a vendor exit, secure continuity of the critical service first, then pursue the commercial dispute in parallel.

questions.subtopic: Log Management. Storage Capacity and Overwrite
questions.question: Log storage for a funds-transfer system is nearly full and is set to overwrite the oldest records. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST response?

options.A: Keep overwriting because recent records matter most to operations
options.B: Halt funds transfers automatically whenever the log storage becomes full
options.C: Delete debug logs to free space for transaction records
options.D: Archive logs to protected storage when a capacity alert fires

questions.key_concept: Log capacity must be monitored with thresholds and archiving, with a predefined, risk-based response if logging fails.
questions.pre_read: Notice what happens to the oldest records. Ask what the two bad outcomes are and how to avoid both.
questions.correct_explanation: Neither silent overwriting nor stopping payments is a good outcome. Alerting at a defined capacity threshold and archiving logs to protected storage keeps the complete audit trail without interrupting transfers. Halting transfers when storage fills does preserve accountability, and may be the right last resort for such a system, but relying on it as the main control turns a predictable storage problem into a business outage.

wrong_explanations.A: Overwriting destroys the oldest records of funds transfers, losing audit trail and evidence without anyone deciding to.
wrong_explanations.B: Halting preserves the trail but turns a foreseeable storage problem into an outage; it is a fallback, not the plan.
wrong_explanations.C: Deleting logs ad hoc frees space once but loses data and does not fix the capacity trend.

tips: Eliminate: A silently loses the audit trail, and C deletes logs ad hoc without fixing capacity.
Final two: D beats B because early alerts and archiving avoid both data loss and outage; halting is the last resort.
Exam cue: plan log capacity so the overwrite-or-halt choice never has to be made.

questions.question: A hotel chain's card processor is down with a 24-hour ETA, and staff process cards manually under the continuity plan; switching processors takes weeks. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the CFO?

options.A: Stop accepting cards and take cash payments until restoration
options.B: Keep the manual card process with cardholder-data controls enforced
options.C: Switch to an alternate processor through emergency procurement
options.D: Let guests settle their bills once the processor is restored

questions.key_concept: Use the tested continuity workaround while keeping its security controls intact; a recovery option slower than the outage adds no value.
questions.pre_read: Compare the 24-hour ETA with the weeks needed to switch. Then check what the continuity plan already provides.
questions.correct_explanation: The continuity plan already provides the manual card process now in use, and it can continue as long as cardholder-data protections still apply to imprint slips and stored card details. An emergency switch sounds decisive, but it takes weeks, well beyond the stated ETA, and rushed integration adds new failure risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Refusing cards turns a manageable outage into lost revenue and guest harm when a planned workaround already exists.
wrong_explanations.C: A switch taking weeks cannot help an outage expected to end within a day, and rushed integration adds risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Deferring payment creates credit and collection risk and ignores the documented continuity procedure already in place.

tips: Eliminate: A gives up card revenue when a planned workaround exists, and D creates credit risk outside the continuity plan.
Final two: B beats C because the planned workaround covers the expected outage, while a weeks-long switch cannot arrive in time.
Exam cue: compare the fix's lead time with the outage's expected duration before choosing a drastic recovery option.

questions.question: Sixteen hours into a breach exposing 340,000 customer records, the incident is still ranked low priority because the priority matrix scores only affected staff users. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Keep the current rating until more staff report problems
options.B: Revise the priority matrix through change control this week
options.C: Reclassify it as a major incident based on business impact
options.D: Brief directors on the attack chain and indicators of compromise

questions.key_concept: Incident priority reflects business impact and urgency; a misfiring priority rule is overridden for the live incident, then corrected.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the matrix measures and what was actually harmed. Ask what the live incident needs right now.
questions.correct_explanation: Priority should reflect business impact, and 340,000 exposed customer records is a major incident however few staff are affected. Reclassifying now triggers the major-incident process: dedicated coordination, escalation and notification clocks. Fixing the matrix through change control is the right follow-up, but doing it first leaves the live breach misranked and under-resourced while the change is approved.

wrong_explanations.A: Staff reports are the wrong measure of impact; customer data exposure is the harm, and waiting leaves the breach under-resourced.
wrong_explanations.B: The matrix needs fixing, but changing it first leaves the live breach misranked and under-resourced while the change is approved.
wrong_explanations.D: Technical detail does not help directors, and briefing them before the incident is properly classified skips the escalation path.

tips: Eliminate: A waits on the wrong measure of impact, and D briefs directors on technical detail before classification.
Final two: C beats B because the live incident needs correct handling now; the matrix fix follows through change control.
Exam cue: classify incidents by business impact; when a rule misfires, override it now and correct it afterward.

questions.question: During ransomware recovery at a federal contractor, IT plans to restore systems in the order they failed, while the BIA ranks payroll and contract billing highest. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Restore systems in the same order they failed
options.B: Restore the most-used systems first to cut help desk calls
options.C: Restore payroll and billing, then directory and shared services
options.D: Restore directory and shared services, then payroll and billing

questions.key_concept: Restoration follows BIA criticality adjusted for technical dependencies: shared infrastructure is recovered first so critical applications can run.
questions.pre_read: Notice the BIA ranks payroll and billing highest. Ask what those applications need running before they can work.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery order follows the BIA's criticality tiers, but critical applications cannot run until the shared services beneath them, such as directory, DNS and databases, are restored and verified clean. Following the tiers with dependencies first gets payroll and billing working soonest. Restoring payroll and billing first matches the BIA ranking, yet without their dependencies they will not start or authenticate.

wrong_explanations.A: Failure order reflects how the attack spread, not business criticality, so critical services may wait behind minor ones.
wrong_explanations.B: Help desk volume is not a recovery criterion; the BIA ranks services by business impact and tolerable downtime.
wrong_explanations.C: The BIA priority is right, but payroll and billing cannot start or authenticate until directory and shared services are back.

tips: Eliminate: A follows the attack's path, and B ranks by help desk noise instead of business impact.
Final two: D beats C because critical applications depend on shared services that must be restored first.
Exam cue: recovery order is BIA priority plus the dependency map; restore foundations before the applications on them.

questions.question: A bug-bounty researcher publicly posts details of an unpatched API flaw on day 47 of the firm's 90-day fix window. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Deploy an emergency mitigation and fast-track the permanent fix
options.B: Notify customers and regulators that a data breach has occurred
options.C: Ask the researcher to take the public post down
options.D: Keep the 90-day schedule because the policy window is still open

questions.key_concept: Public disclosure turns a latent vulnerability into an imminent one: mitigate immediately, then assess impact before any breach notice.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed on day 47. Ask whether the original 90-day window still reflects the real risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Public technical details make exploitation likely within hours, so the risk has changed from latent to imminent. An emergency mitigation reduces exposure now, and fast-tracking the fix closes it. Notifying customers and regulators is transparent, but no breach has been confirmed yet; notice comes after assessing whether data was actually accessed.

wrong_explanations.B: Notice is required once access to data is confirmed. Declared now, before any assessment, it misstates the facts; reduce exposure first, then assess and notify as required.
wrong_explanations.C: Even if the post comes down, copies spread quickly and the flaw stays open, so the exposure is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.D: The internal window assumed the flaw was secret. Public disclosure changes the risk, so the original timeline no longer applies.

tips: Eliminate: C tries to withdraw details already public instead of reducing exposure, and D keeps a timeline that assumed the flaw was secret.
Final two: A beats B because the first priority is to reduce exposure; notification follows once access is actually assessed.
Exam cue: when a flaw's details go public, the fix moves to the emergency change path with interim mitigation; the old fix window no longer applies.
