questions.question: A tax-preparation firm's BIA sets maximum tolerable downtime from impacts measured in July, its quietest month. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the July figures because they reflect normal operations
options.B: Reassess impacts at peak filing season and use the worst case
options.C: Average the impacts across the twelve months of the year
options.D: Set every process to the shortest downtime that any department suggests

questions.key_concept: BIA impact and maximum tolerable downtime must reflect worst-case timing, such as seasonal or cyclical peaks.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the impacts were measured. Ask when an outage would hurt this firm most.
questions.correct_explanation: Impact depends on timing: an outage in July costs little, while the same outage during filing season could be intolerable. The BIA should assess impacts at peak periods and set maximum tolerable downtime from the worst credible timing. Averaging across the year looks balanced, but it still understates peak impact, so recovery would be too slow exactly when the firm can least afford it.

wrong_explanations.A: July impacts understate peak-season losses, so plans sized on them fail when it matters most.
wrong_explanations.C: Averaging does draw on every month, as a fuller BIA should, yet it smooths away filing season; tolerable downtime must hold at the worst credible time.
wrong_explanations.D: Taking the shortest suggestion everywhere ignores real impact and drives unnecessary recovery costs.

tips: Eliminate: A uses the quietest month, and D sets targets by the most demanding opinion.
Final two: B beats C because MTD must hold at the worst credible time; an average hides the peak.
Exam cue: when impact varies by season or cycle, the BIA uses the peak period, not the average.

questions.subtopic: Log Management. Log Integrity and Segregation
questions.question: Operational logs are archived for seven years as evidence, but nothing would reveal whether an archived record had been altered. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Restrict archive access to the central logging team
options.B: Back up the archive monthly to a second storage system
options.C: Seal archived logs with hashes or write-once storage, then verify
options.D: Have internal audit sample archived logs for accuracy each year

questions.key_concept: Archived logs used as evidence need integrity protection, such as hashing or write-once storage with periodic verification, so any alteration is detectable.
questions.pre_read: Notice the logs are kept as evidence. Ask how anyone could prove an archived record is unchanged.
questions.correct_explanation: Logs kept as evidence must be shown to be unaltered. Sealing archives with cryptographic hashes or write-once storage, and verifying them periodically, makes any change impossible or detectable. Restricting access to the logging team narrows who could alter records, but it still relies on trust: if a team member changed a record, nothing would show it, so the archive could not prove its own integrity.

wrong_explanations.A: Fewer people with access lowers the chance of tampering, but an altered record would still go undetected.
wrong_explanations.B: Backups copy whatever the archive holds, including altered records, and prove nothing about integrity.
wrong_explanations.D: An annual sample cannot detect quiet changes, because there is no sealed baseline to compare records against.

tips: Eliminate: B copies records without proving them unchanged, and D samples with nothing to compare against.
Final two: C beats A because sealed archives make changes detectable; restricted access still relies on trusting the team.
Exam cue: log evidence needs integrity protection, such as hashing or write-once storage, not only access control.

questions.question: Management plans to release an endpoint management agent to 2,400 laptops before its 50-laptop pilot finishes. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Hold the release until pilot results and change approval are complete
options.B: Release to one region now and expand as issues are fixed
options.C: Deploy everywhere and roll back any laptops that report problems
options.D: Deploy fleet-wide once the vendor certifies the pilot build

questions.key_concept: A release reaches production only after pilot or test evidence is reviewed and change approval is granted, with a tested backout plan.
questions.pre_read: Notice the pilot has not finished. Ask what a pilot is for and what should gate the release.
questions.correct_explanation: An endpoint agent on every laptop is a high-impact change, so release management requires pilot evidence, formal change approval and a tested backout before deployment. Holding the release secures all three. A regional rollout sounds controlled, but it still pushes an unvalidated build to hundreds of users and makes production staff the test group the pilot was meant to replace.

wrong_explanations.B: Phasing limits blast radius but still deploys a build whose pilot has not finished, so production users become the test group.
wrong_explanations.C: Fleet-wide deployment with reactive rollback assumes a tested backout exists and accepts widespread disruption before problems are known.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor certification shows the build passed the vendor's tests, not that it works on this fleet; the pilot exists to prove that.

tips: Eliminate: C deploys fleet-wide on untested rollback, and D swaps the organization's own pilot evidence for the vendor's word.
Final two: A beats B because a regional rollout still releases an unvalidated build; pilot evidence and approval come first.
Exam cue: a pilot exists to gate the release, so do not release before its results are reviewed and approved.

questions.question: Months later, a colocation provider's SOC 2 report revealed the firm's racks ran on generator power for hours, though every uptime target in the agreement was met. What PRIMARY weakness should the IS auditor report?

options.A: The uptime target written into the agreement is set too low
options.B: The agreement sets no deadline for reporting incidents to the firm
options.C: The provider's monthly service reports exclude facility incidents
options.D: The service credits in the agreement are too small

questions.key_concept: Service levels should include timed incident notification; periodic reports and uptime targets do not tell the customer about events promptly.
questions.pre_read: Notice the gap between when the incident happened and when the firm heard. Ask what controls that timing.
questions.correct_explanation: The delay came from what the agreement requires: it measures uptime but sets no deadline for reporting incidents, so the provider had no duty to tell the firm promptly. Adding timed incident notification to the agreed service levels fixes the cause. Adding facility incidents to the monthly service report helps, but periodic reporting can still leave an incident unreported for weeks; notification must be triggered by the event.

wrong_explanations.A: Uptime measures availability, and every target was met. A higher target would not require the provider to report incidents.
wrong_explanations.C: Monthly reporting would help, but it is periodic, so an incident early in the month could still take weeks to reach the firm.
wrong_explanations.D: Credits compensate for missed targets. None were missed, and larger credits would not make the provider report incidents sooner.

tips: Eliminate: A raises an availability target that was already met, and D enlarges credits when no target was missed.
Final two: B beats C because a reporting deadline is triggered by the event; a monthly report can still arrive weeks later.
Exam cue: if a supplier problem reaches you late, look first at what the agreement requires the supplier to report, and how fast.

questions.subtopic: Generative AI Inadvertently Exposing Customer Data
questions.question: An internal generative AI tool trained on support tickets reveals customer contact details when prompted, once during a vendor demo. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Restrict the tool to senior staff and continue using it
options.B: Add an output filter that masks personal data in responses
options.C: Suspend the tool until the training data is remediated
options.D: Notify every customer in the corpus of a confirmed breach

questions.key_concept: When a system exposes personal data by design, suspend the processing before assessing impact and remediating the root cause.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the personal data lives: in the model itself. Ask which option actually stops it being disclosed.
questions.correct_explanation: The personal data is embedded in the model itself, so every prompt can expose it. Suspending the tool stops further disclosure while the data is assessed and the model retrained on redacted data. An output filter reduces exposure, but filters are routinely bypassed by rephrased prompts, and the data remains in the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Fewer users lowers volume, but anyone with access can still extract customer data from the model.
wrong_explanations.B: Output filtering is a recognized data-loss control for AI tools, yet the data still sits inside the model; contain at the source before patching outputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Notification may be required after assessment, but declaring a confirmed breach to everyone before scoping is premature and does not stop exposure.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the exposure live for fewer users, and D notifies before scoping and does not stop the leak.
Final two: C beats B because the data sits inside the model; a bypassable filter is a half-measure while exposure continues.
Exam cue: when personal data is exposed by design, stop the processing first, then assess, remediate and notify.

questions.question: Daytime CPU use on a shared reporting server nears its limit, and IT requests an urgent hardware upgrade. What should the IS auditor recommend the capacity manager do FIRST?

options.A: Approve the upgrade so users avoid slower daytime reporting
options.B: Move the reporting service to a cloud platform this quarter
options.C: Set a policy limiting each user's daily number of reports
options.D: Analyze the workload to see which jobs could shift off-peak

questions.key_concept: Capacity management includes demand management: analyze and reschedule workload before adding resources.
questions.pre_read: Notice the peak is in the daytime. Ask what is running then and whether it must.
questions.correct_explanation: Capacity management balances supply and demand. Before buying hardware, the capacity manager should analyze what drives the peak; large scheduled reports or extracts can often move to off-peak hours, relieving pressure at little cost. The upgrade may be needed eventually, but approving it first spends money without knowing whether demand management would solve the problem or whether growth will soon outpace the new hardware.

wrong_explanations.A: An upgrade may be needed eventually, but buying before analyzing demand risks spending on a problem scheduling could solve.
wrong_explanations.B: A platform migration is a larger change made without understanding the workload driving the peak.
wrong_explanations.C: Blunt per-user limits ration service without knowing which workloads cause the peak.

tips: Eliminate: B migrates without analysis, and C rations users blindly.
Final two: D beats A because understanding and shifting demand comes before buying more supply.
Exam cue: in capacity questions, analyze the workload and manage demand before adding resources.

questions.question: A hospital's HSM has failed and its untested key escrow cannot be decrypted, leaving seven years of encrypted backup archives unreadable. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Preserve the failed HSM and engage its vendor on recovery
options.B: Declare the archives permanently unrecoverable to the regulator
options.C: Rebuild the archive from the data held in the live systems
options.D: Procure a replacement HSM and generate new backup keys

questions.key_concept: After a key-management failure, preserve the failed device and pursue recovery before declaring loss or taking irreversible steps.
questions.pre_read: Notice that nothing has been tried yet. Ask which option keeps every recovery path open.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery may still be possible: the fault may lie in a component the vendor can repair without erasing the stored keys. Preserving the device and every related artifact keeps that option open before any irreversible step. Procuring a new HSM is needed for future backups, but it does nothing for the archive and may lead to the failed unit being returned or wiped.

wrong_explanations.B: Declaring permanent loss before recovery has been attempted is premature and may misstate the position to the regulator.
wrong_explanations.C: Live systems hold current data, not seven years of history, so most archived records cannot be rebuilt this way.
wrong_explanations.D: New keys protect future backups, but this abandons the archive and risks the failed device being swapped out and wiped.

tips: Eliminate: B gives up before recovery has been tried, and C rebuilds from live systems that do not hold the archived years.
Final two: A beats D because recovery of the archive must be attempted first; the forward fix can follow without destroying options.
Exam cue: when data may be lost, preserve every artifact and attempt recovery before any irreversible action.

questions.subtopic: Year-End Close. Job Scheduling Control Bypass
questions.question: An IS auditor confirms a whistleblower's claim that, during the ongoing year-end close, operators are running ad hoc batch jobs that post journal entries outside the scheduler's approval workflow. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Seek controller approval for each ad hoc run after close
options.B: Block job submission outside the scheduler's approved queue now
options.C: Review the ad hoc runs for unauthorized entries before close
options.D: Rely on the external auditors' year-end testing to cover it

questions.key_concept: Production jobs run only through the scheduler's approved path; when a bypass is active, close it before assessing its impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice the bypass is still happening during close. Ask which step stops the problem growing.
questions.correct_explanation: While the bypass stays open, every new ad hoc run adds unapproved entries to the close, so the first step is to force all job submissions through the scheduler's approval path. Any review then works on a fixed population. Reviewing runs before close is essential, but doing it while operators keep bypassing the workflow means new unapproved entries arrive faster than they are checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval after close does not stop the bypass, and unapproved entries keep posting through year-end into the statements.
wrong_explanations.C: Review is needed, but with the bypass still open, new unapproved runs keep adding entries faster than they can be checked.
wrong_explanations.D: External testing is not the organization's control; relying on it lets unapproved postings continue through close and into the statements.

tips: Eliminate: A approves the bypass after close without stopping it, and D hands the organization's control duty to external auditors.
Final two: B beats C because closing the bypass fixes the population; reviewing first lets new unapproved runs keep arriving.
Exam cue: when a control bypass is still happening, stop the bypass first, then assess what already got through.

questions.question: A firm closing a data center will sell its storage arrays to a reseller. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor that customer data was removed?

options.A: IT staff's confirmation that the array volumes were deleted
options.B: A clause in the reseller's contract requiring it to wipe every drive
options.C: Pre-handover sanitization certificates matched to inventory serial numbers
options.D: Photos of the arrays sealed and leaving the data center

questions.key_concept: Sanitize media before they leave the organization's control, and keep per-drive records reconciled to the asset inventory as evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option proves each drive was sanitized, and whether the data would leave the firm's control first.
questions.correct_explanation: Media should be sanitized, verified and recorded before they leave the organization's control. Certificates tied to drive serial numbers and reconciled to the asset inventory show that every drive was sanitized and none was missed. A contract requiring the reseller to wipe the drives is a useful control, but it is a promise rather than proof, and the data leaves the firm's control before any wipe happens.

wrong_explanations.A: Deleting volumes leaves data recoverable, and a staff statement is weaker evidence than records for each drive.
wrong_explanations.B: A contract clause is a promise, not proof, and the drives would leave the firm's control still holding data.
wrong_explanations.D: Photos show the arrays left the building, not that the data on their drives was removed.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on deletion, which leaves data recoverable, and D shows shipment rather than sanitization.
Final two: C beats B because per-drive records prove sanitization happened; a reseller's contract only promises it, after the data has left.
Exam cue: disposal evidence must tie to each item you control: per-drive records for your own hardware, key-destruction logs for cloud data.

questions.subtopic: DR Site Located in Active-War-Zone Region
questions.question: A bank's DR site lies in a region now suffering attacks on power and telecoms, and switching providers takes six months. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the chief operating officer?

options.A: Keep the current site until the contract renewal date
options.B: Keep the site and add interim capacity while migrating
options.C: Terminate the DR contract and begin migrating immediately
options.D: Rely on the vendor's assurance that operations continue

questions.key_concept: When a recovery site's risk rises but replacement takes months, a staged exit with interim safeguards keeps recovery capability in place.
questions.pre_read: Notice the six-month switching time. Ask what happens to recovery capability while the bank moves.
questions.correct_explanation: The current site is degraded but remains the bank's only recovery capability, and a replacement takes six months. Keeping it while adding interim recovery capacity elsewhere, then moving in stages, holds risk within the BIA objectives until the new site is proven. Terminating at once sounds decisive, but it leaves the bank with no DR capability for the whole six-month switch.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting for renewal adds no safeguards against a material change in risk. Contract timing should not drive a resilience decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Leaving the threatened site is the right destination, yet ending the contract first leaves no recovery option; never drop a control before its replacement works.
wrong_explanations.D: The vendor's self-report is not independent evidence that the site can still meet the BIA recovery objectives.

tips: Eliminate: A lets the contract date drive a resilience decision, and D accepts an interested party's word as evidence.
Final two: B beats C because a staged exit with interim capacity keeps recovery capability; terminating first leaves none for six months.
Exam cue: when the only recovery option is degraded, keep it under compensating safeguards until its replacement is proven.

questions.question: A BIA rates a regulatory reporting process as low priority because it earns no revenue, though a missed filing risks fines and license action. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Include legal and regulatory consequences in the BIA impact criteria
options.B: Keep the rating because revenue is the most objective measure
options.C: Handle missed filings through the compliance team's own procedures
options.D: Insure the process against regulatory fines and penalties

questions.key_concept: BIA impact criteria must include legal and regulatory consequences, not only revenue, so obligation-driven processes get the right priority.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the process was rated low. Ask what else, besides revenue, a missed filing would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: BIA impact criteria should cover all material consequences of disruption, including legal and regulatory ones such as fines, license action and breached obligations, not just lost revenue. Applying those criteria raises the reporting process to its true priority. Leaving missed filings to compliance procedures sounds like clear ownership, but it keeps the process outside continuity planning, so nothing ensures it can recover in time.

wrong_explanations.B: Revenue is easy to measure but is only one impact category; it misses penalties and license risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Compliance can manage regulators, but the process still lacks recovery priority and plans.
wrong_explanations.D: Fines are often uninsurable, and insurance cannot prevent license action or restore the process.

tips: Eliminate: B treats revenue as the only measure of harm, and D tries to insure away an obligation.
Final two: A beats C because the BIA must weigh regulatory impact; handing it to compliance leaves the process without recovery plans.
Exam cue: BIA impact criteria cover financial, legal and regulatory, customer, safety and reputational effects.

questions.question: A post-implementation review finds an acquired firm's legacy ERP still running 11 months after integration because three interfaces depend on it, delaying promised IT savings. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Shut down the legacy ERP now to realize the savings
options.B: Defer decommissioning until the next annual budget cycle is approved
options.C: Retain the legacy ERP as a warm standby for the new platform
options.D: Migrate the three interfaces, then retire it under change control

questions.key_concept: After implementation, legacy systems are retired through change control once dependent interfaces are migrated; untested leftovers are not resilience.
questions.pre_read: Notice what keeps the legacy ERP alive. Ask which option removes that blocker safely.
questions.correct_explanation: The savings depend on retiring the legacy ERP, and the blocker is three live interfaces. Migrating them, then decommissioning through change control with data archived and access removed, delivers the benefit without breaking operations. Keeping the old ERP as a warm standby sounds prudent, but it was never designed or tested for recovery, so it adds cost and stale-data risk rather than real resilience.

wrong_explanations.A: Shutting down now breaks the three interfaces that still depend on the legacy ERP, disrupting order processing to hit a savings date.
wrong_explanations.B: Deferring without a migration plan leaves the dependencies in place, so parallel running and its costs simply continue.
wrong_explanations.C: An auditor would normally welcome a standby, yet one never proven for failover is not recovery capability; untested resilience is only cost.

tips: Eliminate: A breaks live interfaces to hit a savings date, and B defers without removing the dependencies.
Final two: D beats C because a legacy system needs a planned exit, and an untested standby gives no real recovery capability.
Exam cue: retire legacy systems only after their dependencies are migrated, and do it through change control.

questions.subtopic: System Running Unsupported OS for Legacy Reasons
questions.question: A production system runs on an unsupported OS behind network isolation and compensating controls; replacing it costs $8M and 18 months. What is the BEST recommendation the IS auditor should give the CTO?

options.A: Mandate full replacement within six months using compressed validation testing
options.B: Obtain formal management acceptance with a funded exit plan
options.C: Continue operating the system under its existing compensating controls
options.D: Move the system onto a cloud host running the same OS

questions.key_concept: Residual risk from an end-of-support system must be formally accepted by the accountable risk owner and tied to a dated replacement plan.
questions.pre_read: Notice the controls already exist. Ask what is still missing: who owns the residual risk, and when does it end?
questions.correct_explanation: Isolation and compensating controls reduce but do not remove the risk of an unpatchable OS. Management, as risk owner, should formally accept the residual risk and commit funding and dates to replace the system, which also gives regulators and the insurer an accurate position. Continuing under existing controls keeps the system safe today but leaves the risk unowned and with no end date.

wrong_explanations.A: A mandate does not make skipped testing safe; compressed validation risks errors and compliance failures in production.
wrong_explanations.C: The controls help, but without formal acceptance and an exit plan the risk has no accountable owner and no end date.
wrong_explanations.D: Rehosting keeps the same unsupported OS, so the vulnerability and the unowned risk both remain.

tips: Eliminate: A sacrifices required validation for speed, and D moves the unsupported OS without replacing it.
Final two: B beats C because compensating controls need an accountable owner and an end date, not just continuation.
Exam cue: for unsupported systems, look for formal risk acceptance by management plus a replacement plan.

questions.subtopic: Shadow IT. Sanction or Replace Decision
questions.question: An IS auditor finds the sales team adopted an unsanctioned project-tracking SaaS tool that now holds customer data and supports daily work. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Assess the tool and bring it under IT governance
options.B: Order the team to stop using the tool and delete its data
options.C: Accept the tool as is with the sales director's approval
options.D: Buy an enterprise license for the tool across the firm

questions.key_concept: Discovered shadow IT that meets a real need should be risk-assessed, then sanctioned and secured or replaced, rather than banned outright.
questions.pre_read: Notice the tool supports daily work and holds customer data. Ask how to manage both facts at once.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool meets a genuine business need, so the right response is to evaluate its security, contract and data handling, then sanction and secure it or replace it with an approved option. An immediate ban removes the risk on paper, but it disrupts daily sales work, may lose customer records, and teaches staff to hide the next tool rather than disclose it.

wrong_explanations.B: A ban ends the unsanctioned exposure, but when a tool meets a real need, governance assesses it first; a ban may lose records and drives the next tool underground.
wrong_explanations.C: Approval without assessment leaves customer data under unknown security and contract terms.
wrong_explanations.D: A firm-wide license expands use before anyone checks the tool's security, contract or data handling.

tips: Eliminate: C approves the tool without assessing it, and D expands its use before anyone checks its security.
Final two: A beats B because assessment lets the business keep a needed tool safely; a ban disrupts work and drives tools into hiding.
Exam cue: when shadow IT meets a real need, assess it, then sanction or replace it; blocking is a last resort.

questions.question: During a Sev-1 outage, each decision waits 30 minutes for a satellite call to executives, though the incident plan names an incident commander. What is the BEST recommendation the IS auditor should give the COO?

questions.pre_read: Notice the plan already names someone. Ask how to restore speed without losing oversight of the decisions being made.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan already pre-delegates authority to an incident commander, so invoking it removes the 30-minute delay while hourly updates keep executives informed and able to intervene. That is how ITIL incident practice and incident command are meant to work. Letting a senior manager decide alone also restores speed, but it bypasses the defined role and leaves executives blind until the incident closes.

wrong_explanations.A: Per-decision approval by satellite is the cause of the delay. Continuing it extends the outage and the revenue loss.
wrong_explanations.B: Pausing recovery for a committee during a customer-facing outage maximizes business impact. Restoration should continue under delegated authority.
wrong_explanations.C: Speed returns, but decisions bypass the plan's defined role and executives get no visibility until after closure.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the bottleneck causing the delay, and B halts recovery while customers are down.
Final two: D beats C because pre-delegated authority keeps both speed and oversight; ad hoc autonomy loses oversight.
Exam cue: in an incident, use the decision rights the plan already defines rather than inventing new ones.

questions.question: A nightly posting job failed midway, and an operator reran it from the start, posting 3,000 transactions twice. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST control?

options.A: Train operators to escalate failed jobs to the on-call manager
options.B: Run posting jobs during staffed business hours instead
options.C: Define restart points that resume from the last committed record
options.D: Reconcile posted batch totals with the general ledger each month

questions.key_concept: Batch restart and rerun procedures use checkpoints and control totals so failed jobs resume without skipping or duplicating records.
questions.pre_read: Notice the job failed midway and was rerun from the start. Ask what happened to the records already posted.
questions.correct_explanation: Rerunning a partly completed posting job from the start reposts every record already committed. Defined restart points, using checkpoints and control totals, let operators resume from the last committed record, so each transaction posts once. Monthly reconciliation would eventually reveal the duplicates, but only after customers and reports have been affected for weeks; it detects the error rather than preventing it.

wrong_explanations.A: Escalation adds oversight, but without defined restart points the manager faces the same choice and duplicates can still occur.
wrong_explanations.B: Staffed hours do not stop a midway failure or tell anyone where to resume; batch windows usually run overnight for good reasons.
wrong_explanations.D: Prevention beats detection for errors that reach customers. Monthly reconciliation is still a valuable ledger control, yet it finds double postings weeks later.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a person but no restart method, and B moves the job without fixing reruns.
Final two: C beats D because a defined restart point prevents duplicates; monthly reconciliation finds them weeks later.
Exam cue: for failed batch jobs, look for restart and rerun controls that process each record exactly once.

questions.question: BIA questionnaires returned by process owners leave many impact and dependency questions blank or vaguely answered. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST next step?

options.A: Hold follow-up interviews or workshops to validate the responses
options.B: Fill the gaps using the previous year's BIA results
options.C: Have IT complete the missing answers from system documentation
options.D: Send a revised questionnaire with mandatory fields to every owner

questions.key_concept: BIA data from questionnaires should be validated through interviews or workshops with process owners before it is relied on.
questions.pre_read: Notice the answers are blank or vague. Ask how to turn them into reliable results.
questions.correct_explanation: Questionnaires gather data efficiently but often come back with gaps and vague answers. Follow-up interviews or workshops with process owners fill the gaps, clarify impacts against the defined criteria and validate dependencies, producing results management can rely on. A revised questionnaire with mandatory fields may improve completeness, but owners can still answer vaguely, and nobody would challenge or validate their answers.

wrong_explanations.B: Last year's results may be outdated and were never validated against current operations.
wrong_explanations.C: IT documentation describes systems, not the business impact of losing a process.
wrong_explanations.D: Mandatory fields force answers, but not clear or validated ones.

tips: Eliminate: B reuses stale data, and C lets IT guess business impact.
Final two: A beats D because discussion validates and aligns answers; mandatory fields only force a response.
Exam cue: BIA questionnaires are validated through interviews or workshops with process owners.

questions.question: After a year-long operations audit with 38 findings across five areas, each team tracks remediation in its own spreadsheet. With an examination due in six months, what is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep separate team trackers and consolidate them before the exam
options.B: Close each item once its owner confirms the fix is done
options.C: Remediate items in the examination's scope before the others
options.D: Track the findings in one risk-ranked register with retesting

questions.key_concept: Remediation is tracked in one risk-ranked register with owners, target dates and retesting before closure, not by examination scope.
questions.pre_read: Notice the trackers are scattered and an examination is coming. Ask what should set the order of the work.
questions.correct_explanation: Scattered trackers hide overdue and duplicated actions, so one register ranked by risk, with named owners, target dates and retesting before closure, lets management and audit see real progress across all five areas. Remediating examination-scope items first is tempting, but it lets the examiner's agenda override risk and leaves higher-risk issues outside that scope open.

wrong_explanations.A: Consolidating only before the exam keeps progress invisible for months, so slipped or duplicated actions surface too late to fix.
wrong_explanations.B: Owner confirmation is an assertion, not evidence; items need retesting before closure or they may reopen at examination.
wrong_explanations.C: Exam-scope items first would make sense if they were also the highest risks. Remediation order follows risk, not an examiner's agenda, or riskier findings outside that scope wait.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps progress out of view until just before the exam, and B closes items on the owner's word without retesting.
Final two: D beats C because remediation is ordered by risk, not by what examiners plan to look at.
Exam cue: sound remediation tracking means one register, risk ranking, owners, due dates and retesting before closure.

questions.question: During a BIA review, an IS auditor sees management set 24 hours to restore payroll, well inside the 72 hours the business could survive. Which measure does the 24-hour figure MOST directly represent?

options.A: Recovery point objective
options.B: Recovery time objective
options.C: Maximum tolerable period of disruption
options.D: Mean time to repair

questions.key_concept: RTO is the target time to restore a process after disruption; it must sit inside the maximum tolerable period of disruption.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem gives two times. Ask which one is the target management set, and which is the survival limit.
questions.correct_explanation: The recovery time objective is the target elapsed time to restore a process after disruption, set by management through the BIA. Here that is 24 hours. The maximum tolerable period of disruption is the 72-hour survival limit; the RTO must sit inside it to leave a safety margin. Confusing the two would set recovery targets at the edge of business failure.

wrong_explanations.A: RPO measures acceptable data loss, expressed as time before the disruption. It says nothing about how quickly payroll must run again.
wrong_explanations.C: The maximum tolerable period is the 72-hour survival limit in the stem, not the 24-hour restoration target.
wrong_explanations.D: Mean time to repair is a component reliability metric, not a business recovery objective set in a BIA.

tips: Eliminate: A measures data loss, not restoration time, and D is an equipment reliability metric, not a BIA objective.
Final two: B beats C because 24 hours is the restoration target; 72 hours is the survival limit it must sit within.
Exam cue: RTO is the target and maximum tolerable downtime (MTD, called MTPD in ISO 22301) is the cliff edge; the RTO must always be shorter.

questions.question: A BIA sets an eight-hour RTO for order processing, but the business says it cannot survive more than six hours down. Which conclusion should the IS auditor reach as MOST appropriate?

options.A: The RTO is acceptable because it was formally approved
options.B: Recovery testing should be scheduled more often
options.C: The RTO exceeds the maximum tolerable downtime
options.D: The RPO should be shortened to compensate

questions.key_concept: The RTO must be shorter than the maximum tolerable downtime, or recovery completes after the business has failed.
questions.pre_read: Compare the eight-hour RTO with the six hours the business can survive.
questions.correct_explanation: Maximum tolerable downtime is the point beyond which the business cannot survive, so the RTO must be shorter than it, leaving time to resume work. An eight-hour RTO against six hours of tolerable downtime means recovery would finish too late. More frequent testing is useful, but it tests a target that is already wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval does not make an RTO valid if it exceeds what the business can survive.
wrong_explanations.B: Fix the target before testing it. Frequent testing is sound practice, yet it only confirms recovery to an RTO already beyond what the business survives.
wrong_explanations.D: RPO limits data loss; it does not shorten the time to recover.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on approval over substance, and D confuses data loss with downtime.
Final two: C beats B because the target itself is wrong; testing more often does not fix it.
Exam cue: the RTO must always sit inside the maximum tolerable downtime, with a margin to resume work.

questions.question: During a BIA, every department rates all of its processes as critical. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST next step?

options.A: Rank processes enterprise-wide against defined impact criteria
options.B: Accept the ratings because departments know their processes
options.C: Fund recovery for every process at the critical tier
options.D: Let IT decide criticality from system usage statistics

questions.key_concept: A BIA ranks processes against defined, enterprise-wide impact criteria so recovery priorities and funding reflect real business impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice every process is rated critical. Ask what a BIA is supposed to produce from those ratings.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA must set recovery priorities, so processes are ranked across the enterprise against defined impact criteria, such as financial, regulatory and customer impact over time, with senior management agreeing the result. Accepting departmental ratings respects local knowledge, but when everything is critical nothing is prioritized, and recovery funding cannot be allocated sensibly.

wrong_explanations.B: Departments know their processes, but self-rated criticality without shared criteria cannot set priorities.
wrong_explanations.C: Funding everything at the top tier is unaffordable and ignores real differences in impact.
wrong_explanations.D: Usage statistics measure activity, not business impact over time.

tips: Eliminate: C funds every process at the top tier whatever its impact, and D swaps business impact for usage.
Final two: A beats B because shared criteria create real priorities; self-ratings make everything critical.
Exam cue: BIA priorities come from defined impact criteria applied consistently, agreed by senior management.

questions.question: An alternate site is needed for a trading system whose BIA sets a four-hour RTO and near-zero data loss. Which option should the IS auditor recommend as MOST appropriate?

options.A: A reciprocal agreement with a peer firm
options.B: A cold site with power and floor space
options.C: A warm site with preinstalled hardware
options.D: A hot site with current replicated data

questions.key_concept: Alternate site type follows the recovery objectives: short RTO and near-zero RPO need a hot site with current data.
questions.pre_read: Notice both the RTO and the data-loss tolerance. Ask which site meets both, not just one.
questions.correct_explanation: A four-hour RTO with near-zero data loss requires equipment ready to run and data already current, which is what a hot site with replication provides. A warm site has hardware in place, so it looks close, but data must be restored from backups, which takes longer than four hours and loses everything since the last backup.

wrong_explanations.A: Reciprocal agreements are hard to enforce and test, and a peer rarely has spare capacity for a trading load within four hours.
wrong_explanations.B: A cold site needs equipment delivered and installed, which takes days or weeks, far beyond a four-hour RTO.
wrong_explanations.C: Hardware is ready, but data must be restored from backups, breaking both the four-hour RTO and near-zero data loss.

tips: Eliminate: A depends on a peer's unenforceable spare capacity, and B needs equipment installed, taking days or weeks.
Final two: D beats C because only current replicated data meets near-zero data loss; a warm site restores from backup.
Exam cue: match site type to both objectives; short RTO plus tiny RPO means hot.

questions.question: A service desk closes incidents as soon as a fix is applied, and 18% are later reopened. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Measure agents on the number of incidents closed each day
options.B: Reopen every closed incident automatically after 24 hours
options.C: Confirm restoration with the user before closing incidents
options.D: Track the reopen rate monthly without changing closure steps

questions.key_concept: Incidents should be closed only after restoration is confirmed with the user, so failed fixes are not recorded as resolved.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the service desk closes incidents. Ask what the 18% reopen rate says about that moment.
questions.correct_explanation: Under ITIL 4, an incident is resolved when service is restored, and confirming that with the user before closure stops fixes that did not work from being recorded as successes. Tracking the reopen rate gives management visibility, but it measures the failure without changing the closure step that causes it.

wrong_explanations.A: Rewarding closure counts encourages even faster, less verified closures.
wrong_explanations.B: Automatic reopening creates noise and still records unverified fixes as resolved.
wrong_explanations.D: Monitoring the rate shows the problem but leaves its cause in place.

tips: Eliminate: A rewards the behavior causing reopens, and B adds noise without verification.
Final two: C beats D because confirming restoration fixes the cause; tracking only measures it.
Exam cue: incidents close when service is confirmed restored, not when a fix is merely applied.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a critical database server's two disks are mirrored using RAID 1. Which risk does this control MOST directly address?

options.A: Fire destroying the server room
options.B: Failure of a single disk
options.C: Logical corruption of database tables
options.D: Slow writes under heavy transaction load

questions.key_concept: RAID 1 mirrors data across disks so one disk can fail without data loss; it is not a backup and copies logical errors instantly.
questions.pre_read: Notice that mirroring copies every write. Ask what failure that survives, and what it copies straight to the second disk.
questions.correct_explanation: RAID 1 writes identical data to both disks, so the server keeps running if one disk fails, which is the risk it directly addresses. Logical corruption looks covered because data exists twice, but mirroring copies every write, including corrupted ones, to both disks at once. Protecting against corruption needs backups or point-in-time copies, not mirroring.

wrong_explanations.A: Both mirrored disks sit in the same server, so a fire destroys both. Site-level loss needs offsite backups or an alternate site.
wrong_explanations.C: Mirroring sounds like data protection, but it copies every write, corrupt ones included, to both disks at once; only backups or snapshots can undo logical corruption.
wrong_explanations.D: RAID 1 can speed reads, but every write goes to both disks, so it does not address write performance.

tips: Eliminate: A is a site-level loss that destroys both disks, and D is a performance concern RAID 1 does not solve.
Final two: B beats C because mirroring copies corruption to both disks instantly; it protects only against hardware failure.
Exam cue: RAID is availability, not backup; it protects against disk failure, never against bad data.

questions.question: A retailer has replaced its nightly backups with continuous replication to a distant data center. Which risk should the IS auditor report as MOST significant?

options.A: Operators may not yet know the new failover procedure
options.B: Corruption or ransomware would reach both copies at once
options.C: Replication traffic could slow the network during business hours
options.D: The distant site could lose the last few seconds of writes

questions.key_concept: Replication copies corruption and encryption within moments, so it never replaces isolated, point-in-time backups.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a near-instant copy carries besides good data, and what is left if both copies go bad.
questions.correct_explanation: Replication copies every change within moments, including deletions, corruption and ransomware encryption, so both copies can be ruined together and no clean restore point remains. Isolated, point-in-time backups are still needed. Losing the last few seconds of writes is the runner-up: replication over a long distance often carries that small window, but the loss is bounded and usually within the RPO, not the loss of every good copy.

wrong_explanations.A: A new procedure is learned through training and testing; the gap does not leave the retailer without a usable copy of its data.
wrong_explanations.C: Bandwidth affects performance and can be sized or scheduled; it does not threaten the retailer's ability to recover clean data.
wrong_explanations.D: A distant asynchronous copy may lose seconds of writes, but that loss is small and bounded; replicated corruption can leave no clean copy at all.

tips: Eliminate: A is a training gap and C a performance issue; neither leaves the retailer without a clean copy.
Final two: B beats D because a few lost seconds are a bounded loss, while copied corruption can ruin every recoverable version.
Exam cue: replication protects against site loss, not bad data; only isolated, point-in-time backups restore a clean state.

questions.question: An airline's booking database has a five-minute RPO and a one-hour RTO, and its recovery relies on last night's backup plus remote journaling. What is the GREATEST concern for the IS auditor?

options.A: Entries still in transit may exceed the allowed data loss
options.B: Journaling every transaction may slow booking response times
options.C: A corrupted transaction would be copied to the recovery site
options.D: Restore and replay time may exceed the allowed downtime

questions.key_concept: Remote journaling limits data loss, but recovery means restoring the last backup and replaying entries, which takes time against the RTO.
questions.pre_read: Check each objective separately: how much data the method can lose, and how long it takes to run again.
questions.correct_explanation: Journaling keeps loss to seconds, inside the five-minute RPO, but bookings resume only after last night's backup is restored and up to a day of journal entries is replayed. Nothing in the facts shows that this fits inside one hour, so the restore-and-replay window is the greatest risk to the one-hour RTO. A corrupted transaction copied to the recovery site is the runner-up, but point-in-time replay can stop just before it.

wrong_explanations.A: Journaling sends each entry as it happens, so only seconds of work are at risk, well inside a five-minute RPO.
wrong_explanations.B: Journaling overhead can be measured and tuned; it threatens neither recovery objective.
wrong_explanations.C: A copied corrupt transaction is a real journaling risk, but replay can stop just before it, so point-in-time recovery still works; the restore-and-replay time is the open risk.

tips: Eliminate: A overlooks that journaling loses only seconds, and B is a performance issue, not a recovery gap.
Final two: D beats C because replay can stop before a bad transaction, while restoring last night's backup and replaying up to a day of entries may not finish inside a one-hour RTO.
Exam cue: journaling protects the RPO; ask how long restore plus replay takes before trusting it to meet the RTO.

questions.subtopic: Synchronous Replication. Distance, Latency and the RPO Trade-off
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 (Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.14 (Redundancy of Information Processing Facilities); COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity)
questions.question: Synchronous replication to a recovery site 900 miles away has slowed a bank's payment processing. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Upgrade the link between the two sites to higher bandwidth
options.B: Switch to asynchronous replication so payments run faster
options.C: Have the business owner reconfirm the acceptable data loss
options.D: Move the recovery site to a nearby metro-area data center

questions.key_concept: Synchronous replication is limited by distance; moving to asynchronous adds a loss window the business owner must accept first.
questions.pre_read: Ask what limits a write that must be confirmed far away, and who decides how much data loss is acceptable.
questions.correct_explanation: Distance adds delay to every synchronous write, and bandwidth cannot remove it, so the realistic fixes are asynchronous copying, a nearer synchronous site or both. Each trades data loss, cost and regional protection, and the RPO is a business decision, so the business owner must first decide what loss is acceptable. Switching to asynchronous replication is the runner-up: it may be right, but adopting it first quietly changes the RPO.

wrong_explanations.A: More bandwidth does not shorten the travel time of each write over 900 miles, so synchronous writes stay slow.
wrong_explanations.B: Asynchronous copying may be right, but it opens a small data-loss window that the business owner must accept first.
wrong_explanations.D: A nearer site cuts write delay but shares regional disasters; that trade-off, like the RPO, is the business owner's to accept first.

tips: Eliminate: A adds bandwidth, which does not cut distance delay, and D trades regional protection for speed without a business decision.
Final two: C beats B because asynchronous copying changes the RPO, and only the business owner can accept that loss window.
Exam cue: when a recovery design trades data loss for speed or cost, the business owner sets the RPO before IT changes the design.
