questions.pre_read: Ask who must prove recovery works, and whether the contract lets them prove it.
questions.correct_explanation: Using a DRaaS provider does not transfer accountability for recovery. The firm must prove each critical application meets its recovery targets, yet the contract lets it test only two of nine. Securing test rights that cover every critical application, over a planned cycle, closes that gap. The SOC 2 report is the runner-up: it shows the provider's platform controls work, not that this firm's applications recover.

wrong_explanations.A: Service credits compensate after a failed recovery; they give no evidence that the untested applications can be recovered in time.
wrong_explanations.B: More frequent replication reduces data loss, the recovery point, but proves nothing about whether the applications restart in time.
wrong_explanations.C: A SOC 2 report covers the provider's own controls, not whether this firm's applications, data and dependencies recover within its targets.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because service credits only compensate and faster replication only reduces data loss; neither proves recovery.
Final two: D beats C because a SOC 2 report covers the provider's controls, not whether this firm's applications recover in time.
Exam cue: when recovery is outsourced, accountability stays with the customer; prefer the option that lets it test its own recovery.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity); ISO 22301:2019 Clause 8.5 (Exercise Programme); COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cloud Disaster Recovery. DRaaS Contract Review'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4B5.2 (Wave 2 coverage batch Q8: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_181 (cloud backup restore testing left to provider checks), d4_084 (shared hot-site capacity) and d4_228 (data residency): tests that a DRaaS contract must give the customer enough test rights to prove every critical application recovers. Public sources: COBIT 2019, ISO 22301.

questions.question: A service level agreement (SLA) restore target is missed only when the in-house database team must act, and that team handles requests in arrival order. What is the GREATEST weakness the IS auditor should report?

options.A: No internal agreement backs the SLA with set response times
options.B: The restore target is stricter than recent results support
options.C: Missed targets are not reported to the business each month
options.D: The agreement sets no service credits for missed targets

questions.key_concept: Internal teams behind a service level agreement (SLA) need operational level agreements (OLAs) whose times fit within the SLA target.
questions.pre_read: Find where in the chain the target is lost, then ask what commits that link to a time.
questions.correct_explanation: An SLA target is achievable only if every team behind it is committed to supporting times. Here the database team works in arrival order with no operational level agreement (OLA), so its delays break the end-to-end target. A target stricter than recent results is the runner-up: targets come from business need, so the fix is an OLA, not a lower target.

wrong_explanations.B: Targets come from business need, not from what IT achieves today; lowering one would hide the gap rather than fix its cause.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting misses tells the business about the problem but does nothing about why the database work is slow.
wrong_explanations.D: Service credits move money after a miss; they do not commit the database team to act within the time the target needs.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because reporting misses and service credits react after a failure; neither commits the team that causes it.
Final two: A beats B because the target reflects business need; lowering it hides the gap instead of fixing the missing commitment.
Exam cue: when an SLA fails at one internal handoff, look for a missing operational level agreement (OLA).
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Service Level Management practice; COBIT 2019 APO09 (Managed Service Agreements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Service Levels. Missed Restore Targets'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A10.1 (Wave 2 coverage batch Q8: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_003 (measurable targets), d4_165 (balanced metrics), d4_171 and d4_180 (measuring and reconciling performance) and d4_246 (incident notification): tests that internal teams behind an SLA need OLAs that support its targets. Public sources: ITIL 4, COBIT 2019. D4 difficulty upgrade (Oct 2026, owner's rule: eliminations fall to CISA knowledge, final two decided by the ISACA lens): Gap-echo: the key no longer repeats 'database team'.

questions.question: A hosting provider misses the four-hour restore target in its service level agreements (SLAs) because its hardware supplier's contract allows next-day repair. Which control should the IS auditor consider MOST effective against such gaps?

options.A: Annual surveys of customer satisfaction with restore times
options.B: A check of supplier terms against SLA targets before signing
options.C: Monthly SLA performance reports reviewed with each customer
options.D: Supplier penalties that match the service credits owed to customers

questions.key_concept: Underpinning contracts with suppliers must support the service level agreement (SLA) targets they sit behind; check both before signing, as penalties do not restore service.
questions.pre_read: Separate controls that prevent a mismatch from ones that report it or pay for it afterward.
questions.correct_explanation: The provider promised a four-hour restore that its underpinning contract with the hardware supplier cannot support. The preventive control is to check each supplier contract against the SLA targets it underpins before either is signed or renewed, so the commitments line up. Matching penalties are the runner-up: they pass the financial cost to the supplier, but repairs still take until the next day.

wrong_explanations.A: Surveys show unhappy customers after the fact; they do not stop the provider promising targets its suppliers cannot support.
wrong_explanations.C: Performance reports detect missed targets after they happen; the mismatch with the supplier's terms would remain.
wrong_explanations.D: Matching penalties recover money, but repairs would still take until the next day, so the four-hour target would keep failing.

tips: Eliminate: A and C, because surveys and performance reports only show the misses after customers have suffered them.
Final two: B beats D because matching penalties recover money while repairs still take a day; aligned terms stop the gap forming.
Exam cue: service credits and penalties transfer cost, not service; prefer controls that align commitments before signing.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO09 (Managed Service Agreements); ITIL 4 Supplier Management practice; ITIL 4 Service Level Management practice; COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Service Levels. Hosting Provider Gaps'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A10.1 (Wave 2 coverage batch Q8: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_171 (independent measurement of provider figures), d4_180 (metric disputes) and d4_246 (incident notification terms): tests aligning underpinning supplier contracts with SLA targets before signing, rather than relying on matching penalties. Public sources: COBIT 2019, ITIL 4.

questions.question: With Sunday full backups and daily incrementals, Monday restores take six hours and Saturday's take 12, against an eight-hour recovery time objective (RTO). Which change would the IS auditor consider MOST LIKELY to fix this?

options.A: Verify each incremental backup as it is written
options.B: Take incremental backups every four hours instead
options.C: Replace the daily incrementals with daily differentials
options.D: Move the weekly full backup from Sunday to Wednesday night

questions.key_concept: Incremental restores apply the full plus every later set in order; differentials need only the full plus the latest set, shortening late-cycle restores.
questions.pre_read: Work out how many backup sets each restore must apply, and how each option changes that count.
questions.correct_explanation: Restore time grows each day because each incremental must be loaded in order after the full backup. A differential holds every change since the full, so any restore needs the full plus one set, with no six-set chain and no record restored several times. That makes it the change most likely to bring Saturday under eight hours. Moving the full to Wednesday is the runner-up, but the day before it still needs six incrementals.

wrong_explanations.A: Verifying each incremental checks its integrity, but a Saturday restore would still apply the full backup plus six sets in order.
wrong_explanations.B: Four-hourly incrementals improve the recovery point but multiply the sets a restore must apply, making late-week restores even slower.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving the full backup only moves the long chain; a restore on the day before the new full would still apply six incrementals.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because verification does not shorten a restore and more frequent incrementals add sets to apply.
Final two: C beats D because moving the full only shifts the chain; the day before it still needs six incrementals.
Exam cue: restores that slow as the week goes on point to a long incremental chain; differentials cut it to one set.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.13 (Information Backup); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-9 (System Backup)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Backup Schemes. Weekly Cycle'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4B3.1 (Wave 2 coverage batch Q8: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_061 (identifying a differential scheme from its restore pattern) and d4_075 (a bad incremental found in testing): tests how the incremental chain stretches late-week restores past the RTO and how differentials shorten it. Public sources: ISO/IEC 27002:2022, NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5.

questions.question: A payroll bureau reuses backup media every 14 days, and its records show data errors usually surface four to six weeks after they occur. Which is the GREATEST risk for the IS auditor to report?

options.A: Older payroll periods unavailable for legal or audit requests
options.B: Ransomware encrypting the backups along with the live data
options.C: Losing up to 14 days of payroll changes in a failure
options.D: Every clean copy being overwritten before an error is found

questions.key_concept: Backup retention must outlast the usual time to detect data errors, or every remaining copy may already hold the bad data.
questions.pre_read: Compare how long backups are kept with how long problems take to come to light.
questions.correct_explanation: Retention must outlast the time errors usually take to be noticed. Here media is reused after 14 days, but errors surface four to six weeks later, so by then every backup already holds the bad data and no clean restore point exists. Losing 14 days of changes is the runner-up, but it confuses media reuse with backup frequency.

wrong_explanations.A: Legal retention is usually met by separate archives; the facts point to recovery, where every recent copy holds the errors.
wrong_explanations.B: Ransomware is a real threat to backups, but nothing here points to it; the facts given show clean copies overwritten before errors appear.
wrong_explanations.C: Reusing media every 14 days sets how long copies are kept, not how often backups run; the backup schedule decides how much recent data is lost.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because legal history sits in separate archives and nothing in the facts points to ransomware.
Final two: D beats C because 14-day reuse limits how long copies are kept, not how often they are taken.
Exam cue: when errors come to light weeks after they occur, check that backup retention outlasts that detection time.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.13 (Information Backup); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-9 (System Backup)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Backup Rotation. Media Reuse Cycle'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4B3.1 (Wave 2 coverage batch Q8: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_233 (responding once corruption is found and backups have rotated out), d4_064 (rotation for seven-year legal retention) and d4_162 (immutable copies): tests designing retention to outlast the usual time to detect data errors. Public sources: ISO/IEC 27002:2022, NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5.

questions.question: A logistics firm restores a few sample files from backup each month without errors, and its shipment-tracking database has a 10-hour recovery time objective (RTO). Which evidence should the IS auditor consider MOST relevant?

options.A: Results of a timed restore of the whole database
options.B: Checksums comparing each restored sample file with its source
options.C: Logs showing every nightly database backup job completed
options.D: The backup vendor's published maximum restore speeds

questions.key_concept: Restore tests must be timed and sized like a real recovery; small sample restores cannot show whether the recovery time objective (RTO) is achievable.
questions.pre_read: Identify the target the stem gives, then pick the evidence that tests that target directly.
questions.correct_explanation: Successful sample restores show some files can come back, but the tracking database has a 10-hour RTO and nobody knows whether a full restore fits. Only a timed restore of the complete database, on realistic hardware, shows whether recovery meets the target. Checksums on the samples are the runner-up: they confirm small files are intact, not the time needed to recover the system that matters.

wrong_explanations.B: Checksums show the sample files came back intact, but samples say nothing about how long the whole database would take to restore.
wrong_explanations.C: Job logs show data was written, not that it restores, and not how long a restore would take.
wrong_explanations.D: Published speeds are vendor claims under ideal conditions; they are not evidence of this firm's actual restore time.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because job logs and vendor speed claims show neither that data restores nor how long it takes here.
Final two: A beats B because checksums prove sample files are intact, not that the whole database restores within 10 hours.
Exam cue: when a stem states a recovery time objective, the best restore evidence is a timed restore at full scale.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8 Safeguard 11.5 (Test Data Recovery); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Restore Testing. Monthly Sample Restores'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4B3.4 (Wave 2 coverage batch Q8: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_075 (checksums on restored data), d4_126 (restores from offsite media), d4_181 (cloud restore testing ownership) and d4_222 (directory restores): tests that restore tests must be timed at full scale to show the RTO is achievable. Public sources: CIS Controls v8, NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5.

questions.question: The operations team gives the IS auditor signed reports of quarterly restore tests that the backup administrator chose and ran. Which further step would provide the BEST evidence that backups can be restored?

options.A: Inspect backup job logs covering the same quarters
options.B: Observe restores of backup sets the IS auditor picks
options.C: Confirm that a manager approved each signed test report
options.D: Obtain the backup vendor's statement of product reliability

questions.key_concept: Evidence the IS auditor obtains directly from an independently selected sample is more reliable than reports produced by the person being audited.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chose what was tested, and who would produce each piece of evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence the IS auditor obtains directly, from a sample the IS auditor selects, is more reliable than reports prepared by the person whose work is being tested. Observing restores of independently picked backup sets removes the risk that only known-good sets were tested. Manager approval of the reports is the runner-up: it adds a review, but the administrator still chose and ran every test.

wrong_explanations.A: Job logs show backups were written, not that they restore; they add nothing to the test reports already provided.
wrong_explanations.C: Manager approval adds a review, but the administrator still chose and ran every test, so the selection bias remains.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor's reliability claim covers its product in general, not whether this firm's backup sets restore.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because job logs and vendor claims show nothing about whether this firm's backup sets restore.
Final two: B beats C because approval still leaves the administrator's own choice of tests; sets the IS auditor picks remove that bias.
Exam cue: when evidence comes from the person being audited, prefer evidence the IS auditor obtains or observes directly.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); CIS Controls v8 Safeguard 11.5 (Test Data Recovery)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Restore Testing. Audit Evidence'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4B3.4 (Wave 2 coverage batch Q8: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_126 (adding restores to a contract-only control) and d4_075 (checksums on restored data): tests the reliability of restore-test evidence prepared by the administrator against restores of sets the IS auditor selects and observes. Public sources: ISACA ITAF, CIS Controls v8.

questions.subtopic: Availability Measurement. Verifying a Reported Figure
questions.question: The IT operations manager reports 99.95% quarterly availability for a claims system, taken from the monitoring team's own dashboard. Which procedure would give the IS auditor the BEST evidence that the figure is accurate?

options.A: Review the dashboard tool's settings and alert thresholds
options.B: Obtain the operations manager's signed confirmation of the figure
options.C: Compare the figure with the availability reported in the previous quarter
options.D: Recalculate the figure from incident records of each outage's duration

questions.key_concept: Reperforming a reported metric from independent source records gives stronger evidence than reviewing the tool or the people that produced it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced the figure, and which independent records would let the IS auditor rebuild it.
questions.correct_explanation: Reperformance gives the strongest evidence: the IS auditor rebuilds the figure from incident records showing when each outage started and ended, independent of the dashboard that produced it. Missed or excluded outages then show up as differences. Reviewing the tool's settings is the runner-up: it shows how the dashboard measures, but not whether this quarter's figure is right.

wrong_explanations.A: Settings show how the dashboard measures availability, not whether this quarter's figure is correct; outages the tool missed would stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.B: A confirmation from the person reporting the figure adds no independent evidence; it simply restates management's claim.
wrong_explanations.C: A comparison with last quarter shows a trend, not whether either quarter's figure is accurate.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because a manager's confirmation restates the claim and a trend comparison cannot show either figure is right.
Final two: D beats A because rebuilding the figure from incident records tests the number itself; reviewing settings only tests the tool.
Exam cue: to verify a reported metric, prefer reperforming it from independent source records over reviewing whoever or whatever produced it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); COBIT 2019 BAI04 (Managed Availability and Capacity); ITIL 4 Measurement and Reporting practice
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Availability Measurement. Verifying a Reported Figure'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A6.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_032 (synthetic transactions), d4_143 (maintenance excluded from service hours), d4_180 (reconciling customer and provider figures with the contract) and d4_019 (outage timeline for root cause): tests reperforming a self-reported availability figure from incident records. Public sources: ISACA ITAF, COBIT 2019, ITIL 4.

questions.question: A warehouse system fails twice a year, and each repair takes two days while parts ship, though the business tolerates only four-hour outages. Which recommendation should the IS auditor consider MOST cost-effective?

options.A: Hold critical spare parts on site with tested repair steps
options.B: Build a redundant second site that fails over automatically
options.C: Replace components more often under a planned preventive maintenance program
options.D: Report availability without the time spent waiting for parts

questions.key_concept: Availability rises by failing less often or recovering faster; fix the factor that actually drives downtime, at a cost matched to business need.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the downtime comes from how often the system fails or from how long each repair takes.
questions.correct_explanation: Downtime here comes from slow repair, not frequent failure, so the cheapest fix is cutting mean time to repair. Spare parts on site and tested repair steps can bring each outage within the four-hour tolerance. A redundant site with automatic failover is the runner-up: it would also meet the need, but at a cost far beyond what two failures a year justify.

wrong_explanations.B: Automatic failover would meet the tolerance, but its cost far exceeds what is needed when faster repair alone fixes the problem.
wrong_explanations.C: Preventive maintenance cuts how often failures happen; failures are already rare, and each one would still take two days to fix.
wrong_explanations.D: Leaving parts delays out of the figure hides downtime instead of reducing it; the business would still face two-day outages.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because preventive maintenance targets failures that are already rare, and changing the report removes downtime from the figure, not from the business.
Final two: A beats B because faster repair alone meets the four-hour tolerance; a failover site buys resilience the business does not need.
Exam cue: split downtime into how often and how long; recommend the cheapest fix for the factor that breaks the business tolerance.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI04 (Managed Availability and Capacity); COBIT 2019 DSS01 (Managed Operations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Availability Improvement. Long Repair Times'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A6.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_154 (interpreting MTTR and MTBF trends) and d4_041 (setting targets from business impact): tests choosing the improvement by the factor that drives downtime, at a cost matched to tolerance. Public sources: COBIT 2019. D4 difficulty upgrade (Oct 2026, owner's rule: eliminations fall to CISA knowledge, final two decided by the ISACA lens): Eliminate tip no longer uses dismissive wording.

questions.subtopic: Log Coverage. Testing Completeness of Log Sources
questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that every production server sends logs to the central log store. Which procedure would MOST LIKELY reveal servers that were never connected to it?

options.A: Review source-health alerts for log sources that stopped sending
options.B: Compare the server inventory with sources reporting to the log store
options.C: Inspect the approved logging standard's list of required log sources
options.D: Trace a sample of log store alerts back to their servers

questions.key_concept: Completeness is tested from the full population toward the records; a server that never sent logs leaves nothing in the log store to find.
questions.pre_read: Ask which direction each test runs, and whether it could find something that left no trace at all.
questions.correct_explanation: To find servers that never sent logs, the IS auditor must start from the full population, the server inventory, and check each server against the sources reporting to the log store. Anything missing shows up as a gap. Source-health alerts are the runner-up: they flag sources that stop sending, but a server never connected was never expected, so it raises no alert.

wrong_explanations.A: Source-health alerts cover only sources the log store expects; a server that was never connected raises no alert at all.
wrong_explanations.C: A standard shows which sources should send logs, not which servers actually do; it is design evidence only.
wrong_explanations.D: Tracing alerts starts from logs that already arrive, so it cannot reveal servers that send nothing.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because a standard shows only intended sources, and tracing alerts starts from logs that already arrive.
Final two: B beats A because source-health alerts watch only sources already configured; the inventory shows servers the log store never knew.
Exam cue: to prove completeness, test from the full population toward the records; tests that start from the records cannot find what is missing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-92 (Guide to Computer Security Log Management); CIS Controls v8 Control 8 (Audit Log Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-8 (System Component Inventory)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Log Coverage. Testing Completeness of Log Sources'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A9.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_163 (finding that network segments send no data), d4_035 (operating system and database logs overwritten) and the 4A9.2 source-health control: tests the completeness procedure, from inventory to log sources. Public sources: NIST SP 800-92, CIS Controls v8, NIST SP 800-53.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a firm keeps its public cloud account's activity log only for the provider's short default period and never exports it. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Operating system events on the firm's cloud servers would go unrecorded
options.B: Errors inside the firm's cloud-hosted applications would go unrecorded
options.C: Older changes to cloud resources and permissions could not be traced
options.D: The firm could not check the provider's monthly usage charges

questions.key_concept: Each layer keeps its own log; in the cloud, the account activity log is the only record of who changed resources and access rights.
questions.pre_read: Ask which layer the missing log covers, and which actions happen only at that layer.
questions.correct_explanation: A cloud account's activity log records management actions: who created, changed or deleted servers, storage, network rules and access rights, through the console or programming interfaces. Providers keep only a short default history, so without a trail exported to the firm's own store, older changes by an administrator or attacker cannot be traced. Unrecorded operating system events are the runner-up, but those are logged on each server separately, not by the account activity log.

wrong_explanations.A: Operating system events are logged on each server by its own logging; the account activity log covers management actions, not server internals.
wrong_explanations.B: Application errors go to each application's own log, not the account activity log.
wrong_explanations.D: Usage charges come from the provider's billing records, which exist however long the activity log is kept.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because application errors go to each application's own log, and billing records exist however long the activity log is kept.
Final two: C beats A because server events are logged on each server; only the account activity log records changes to resources and access.
Exam cue: map each missing log to its layer; the biggest risk is losing the only record of actions taken at that layer.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-2 (Event Logging); CIS Benchmarks (AWS/Azure/GCP Foundations); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.15 (Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Log Coverage. Cloud Account Activity Log Retention'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A9.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_163 and d4_035 (on-premises layers not logged) and d5_154 and d5_279 (restoring console changes from the code baseline): tests that the cloud management layer's activity log must be exported and kept beyond the provider's short default. Public sources: NIST SP 800-53, CIS Foundations Benchmarks, ISO/IEC 27002.

questions.subtopic: Configuration Baselines. Baseline Taken From Live Settings
questions.question: A retailer installs a configuration drift tool on its payment servers and saves each server's settings on installation day as its baseline. What should the IS auditor consider the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Settings that were already insecure would never raise an alert
options.B: Approved later changes would raise alerts until baselines are updated
options.C: Configuration scans could slow the payment servers at peak hours
options.D: Server changes would no longer need change tickets or approval

questions.key_concept: A baseline must be the approved, secure configuration; capturing whatever is running makes existing weaknesses the standard that drift is measured against.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the baseline was checked against before it was accepted as correct.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift detection only reports differences from the baseline. If the baseline is whatever each server ran on installation day, any insecure or unauthorized setting already present becomes the standard and is never flagged. The baseline should be an approved secure configuration. Alerts on later approved changes are the runner-up: they are noise, managed by updating baselines through change management, not a hidden weakness.

wrong_explanations.B: Updating baselines after approved changes is routine upkeep; the extra alerts are manageable noise, not an undetected weakness.
wrong_explanations.C: Scans can be scheduled and tuned; possible load on the servers is an operational detail, not a gap in configuration control.
wrong_explanations.D: Drift detection checks changes after they happen; it never replaces approval, so change tickets are still required.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because scan load can be scheduled, and drift detection never replaces change approval.
Final two: A beats B because alerts on approved changes are fixable noise, while a baseline copied from live settings hides existing weaknesses.
Exam cue: a detective control is only as good as its reference point; ask who approved the baseline before trusting a clean drift report.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration); NIST SP 800-128 (Security-Focused Configuration Management); COBIT 2019 BAI10 (Managed Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Configuration Baselines. Baseline Taken From Live Settings'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A8.2 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_155 (drift alerts against change tickets as evidence) and d5_048 (scanning hardened servers against their baseline); shares the reference-point principle of d5_300 (an intrusion detection baseline learned during an attack) but tests it in configuration management. Public sources: NIST SP 800-53, NIST SP 800-128, COBIT 2019.

questions.question: Drift alerts on a bank's production servers go to the operations team, who close each with a brief comment and no change record. What is the PRIMARY weakness for the IS auditor to report?

options.A: Alerts are not escalated to the security team for review
options.B: Alert comments do not follow a standard written format
options.C: The tool reports changes after they are made, not before
options.D: Closed alerts are not traced to an authorized request

questions.key_concept: Drift detection works only when every alert is traced to an authorized change; unexplained differences are investigated and reversed.
questions.pre_read: Ask which step turns an alert into a conclusion about whether the change was allowed.
questions.correct_explanation: A drift alert shows only that something changed. The control works when each alert is traced to an authorized change request, and differences with no request are investigated and reversed. Closing alerts with a comment lets an unauthorized change pass as explained. Escalating alerts to the security team is the runner-up: it adds reviewers, but still no one confirms each change was allowed.

wrong_explanations.A: Escalation adds reviewers, but without matching each alert to an authorized request, no one confirms the change was allowed.
wrong_explanations.B: A standard comment format tidies the record but still would not show whether each change was authorized.
wrong_explanations.C: Drift detection is detective by design; preventing changes is the job of access and change controls, not this tool.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because comment format is cosmetic, and drift tools are meant to detect changes after they happen.
Final two: D beats A because escalation adds reviewers but never confirms each change was authorized; tracing to a request does.
Exam cue: monitoring without a response step is a weak control; look for the option that closes each alert against an authorization.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-128 (Security-Focused Configuration Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); COBIT 2019 BAI10 (Managed Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Configuration Management. Handling Drift Alerts'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A8.2 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_155 (which evidence shows no change happened outside the process) and d4_311 (where the baseline comes from): tests that each drift alert must be closed against an authorized change. Public sources: NIST SP 800-128, NIST SP 800-53, COBIT 2019.

questions.subtopic: Operating System Hardening. Extra Services on a New Server
questions.question: A newly built file server has remote shell, web and print services running, although it only shares department files. Which recommendation should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Block the extra services' ports at the network firewall
options.B: Patch the extra services to the vendor's latest versions
options.C: Disable the services the file-sharing function does not use
options.D: Check the extra services' logs each week for any misuse

questions.key_concept: Least functionality: remove services a system's function does not need rather than shield them; what is not running cannot be attacked.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each option removes the exposure or only places a guard in front of it.
questions.correct_explanation: A hardened baseline runs only the services a server's function needs. Disabling the remote shell, web and print services removes their attack surface entirely, so future flaws in them cannot be exploited. Blocking their ports at the firewall is the runner-up: it shields one path, but the services still run and stay reachable from inside the network or if a rule changes.

wrong_explanations.A: Firewall blocking shields one path only; the services still run and stay reachable from inside the network or after a rule change.
wrong_explanations.B: Patching fixes known flaws but keeps services the server does not need, so future flaws remain exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: Log review may detect misuse after it happens; it does not remove the exposure the extra services create.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because patching keeps unneeded services exposed to future flaws, and log review only finds misuse afterward.
Final two: C beats A because a firewall rule only shields the services; disabling them removes the exposure entirely.
Exam cue: when a system runs something its function does not need, prefer removing it over guarding, patching or watching it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-7 (Least Functionality); NIST SP 800-123 (Guide to General Server Security); CIS Benchmarks for Operating Systems
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Operating System Hardening. Extra Services on a New Server'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A1.4 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_045 (vendor defaults replaced by a hardened baseline), d4_057 (hardening that breaks operations) and d5_048 (scanning to keep hardening in place): tests removing unneeded services rather than shielding them. Public sources: NIST SP 800-53, NIST SP 800-123, CIS Benchmarks.

questions.subtopic: Utility Programs. Unknown Utilities on Production Servers
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that no one at a hospital can say which data-editing and disk utilities are installed on its production servers. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Restrict each utility to named administrators through approved requests
options.B: Remove every utility program from the production servers at once
options.C: Inventory each server's utilities and who can run them
options.D: Log every utility session for a monthly security review

questions.key_concept: Control starts with knowing what exists: identify privileged utilities and who can run them before restricting, logging or removing them.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each control could be applied yet, given what the organization currently knows.
questions.correct_explanation: Utilities can change data directly and skip application controls, so they belong with named administrators. But no one knows which utilities exist or who can run them, so the first step is an inventory of each server's utilities and their users. Restricting utilities to named administrators is the runner-up: it is the right control, but it cannot be applied to tools nobody has identified.

wrong_explanations.A: Restriction is the right control, but it cannot be applied to utilities nobody has identified; the inventory must come first.
wrong_explanations.B: Administrators need some utilities for maintenance and recovery; removing them blindly could disrupt clinical systems. Control them instead.
wrong_explanations.D: Logging finds misuse only after data has changed, and it cannot cover utilities nobody knows are installed.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because blanket removal disrupts needed administration, and logging only finds misuse after data has changed.
Final two: C beats A because restriction is the right control but needs a list of utilities and users to apply to.
Exam cue: with FIRST, ask what must be known before any control can work; an inventory usually comes before restriction or monitoring.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.18 (Use of Privileged Utility Programs); CIS Controls v8 Control 2 (Inventory and Control of Software Assets)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Utility Programs. Unknown Utilities on Production Servers'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A1.4 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_030 (restricting a known utility), d4_168 (a finding in utility logs) and d4_149 (spreadsheet inventory): tests that unknown utilities must be identified before any control can be applied. Public sources: ISO/IEC 27002, CIS Controls v8.

questions.subtopic: Shadow IT Discovery. Remote Staff Outside the Proxy
questions.question: An IS auditor is measuring shadow IT from proxy logs, but most staff work from home without passing through the proxy. Which additional evidence would MOST LIKELY reveal the unsanctioned services they use?

options.A: Survey responses from department heads listing the tools in use
options.B: Corporate card and expense records of software subscriptions
options.C: Single sign-on logs for the applications IT has configured
options.D: Help desk tickets that mention problems with unapproved tools

questions.key_concept: When one evidence source has a blind spot, use an independent source it does not affect; payments for cloud services appear wherever staff work.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each source can see, and whether working from home hides the services from it.
questions.correct_explanation: Paid cloud services leave a financial trail wherever staff work: card charges and expense claims for subscriptions show unsanctioned services the proxy never saw. Free services leave no payment trail, so this adds to other sources rather than replacing them. Single sign-on logs are the runner-up: they are reliable records, but they cover only applications IT has configured, which are sanctioned by definition.

wrong_explanations.A: Self-reported lists under-report, because people forget tools or choose not to declare them; independent records are more reliable.
wrong_explanations.C: Single sign-on covers only applications IT has set up, which are sanctioned by definition.
wrong_explanations.D: Tickets capture only tools that fail and that someone chooses to report, a small and biased part of actual use.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because surveys rely on people declaring their own tools and tickets capture only tools that break.
Final two: B beats C because sign-on logs cover only applications IT configured, while payments for paid services show up wherever staff work.
Exam cue: when one evidence source has a blind spot, choose an independent source that the blind spot does not affect.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Shadow IT Discovery. Remote Staff Outside the Proxy'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A5.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_012 (proxy and CASB logs over a survey), d4_018 (risk-ranking services found) and d2_156 (shadow APIs): tests choosing evidence that the proxy's remote-work blind spot does not affect. Public sources: COBIT 2019, ISACA ITAF.

questions.subtopic: Shadow IT. Service Registered to a Personal Account
questions.question: A business unit's unsanctioned file-sharing service, which holds client contracts, was registered by a project manager using a personal email address. What is the PRIMARY risk for the IS auditor to report?

options.A: Control of the contracts could be lost when the manager leaves
options.B: Subscription fees for the service are paid outside the IT budget
options.C: The service may not enforce sign-in rules protecting the contracts
options.D: The service does not appear in the firm's software inventory

questions.key_concept: Data in a service the organization does not own or administer is outside its control; ownership comes before any other control on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who could access, recover or delete the data tomorrow if the person who set it up left.
questions.correct_explanation: The account belongs to an individual, not the firm, so the firm has no administrative or contractual control over the client contracts in it. If the manager leaves or loses access, the firm may be unable to retrieve, preserve or delete them. Weak sign-in rules are the runner-up: they matter, but the firm could not enforce any control on an account it does not own.

wrong_explanations.B: Paying fees outside the IT budget is a spending governance issue; it does not put the client contracts at risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Weak sign-in rules matter, but the firm cannot enforce any rule on an account it does not own; ownership comes first.
wrong_explanations.D: A missing inventory entry is a symptom of shadow IT, not the main risk to the client contracts held in the service.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because budget coding and inventory records are governance gaps that do not threaten the contracts themselves.
Final two: A beats C because the firm cannot enforce sign-in rules on an account it does not own; losing control of the data comes first.
Exam cue: for shadow IT, ask who owns the account and the data; without ownership, no other control can be enforced.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.23 (Information Security for Use of Cloud Services); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Shadow IT. Service Registered to a Personal Account'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A5.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_256 (sanctioning a useful tool), d4_018 (risk-ranking many services) and d4_213 (batch jobs under a leaver's account): tests that a service owned by an individual leaves the firm without control of its data. Public sources: ISO/IEC 27002, COBIT 2019.

questions.subtopic: Database Models. Moving From Relational to Document Storage
questions.question: A retailer is moving its customer master data from a relational database to a document store that does not require a fixed schema. What should the IS auditor review FIRST?

options.A: Reconciliation of record counts between the old and new systems
options.B: Staff skills for administering the new document store
options.C: Query response times of the new store under peak load
options.D: Where each old table constraint will now be enforced

questions.key_concept: When a database stops enforcing structure by default, its integrity rules must be rebuilt elsewhere; the IS auditor checks where each one went.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the old database did automatically that the new one will not.
questions.correct_explanation: The relational database enforced keys, required fields and allowed values on every write. A document store without a fixed schema enforces none of these by default, so each rule must be rebuilt in the application or the store's own validation rules, or it is silently lost. Mapping where each constraint will be enforced comes first. Reconciling record counts is the runner-up: it proves the one-time move was complete, not that later records stay valid.

wrong_explanations.A: Count reconciliation confirms the one-time move was complete, but it cannot show that records written afterward obey the old rules.
wrong_explanations.B: Administration skills affect operations, but no amount of skill restores integrity rules the new store does not enforce by default.
wrong_explanations.C: Query speed is a performance question; fast queries say nothing about whether stored customer data stays valid.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because skills and query speed are operational concerns that do not protect the data's integrity.
Final two: D beats A because count reconciliation checks only the one-time move; lost constraints let every later write store invalid data.
Exam cue: when a control moves out of the database, look for where it lands; integrity rules not rebuilt elsewhere are lost.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); DAMA-DMBOK 2nd Edition (Data Modeling and Design, Data Storage and Operations); COBIT 2019 BAI03 (Managed Solutions Identification and Build)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Database Models. Moving From Relational to Document Storage'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A11.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_042 (the risk of a schema-less store), d4_055 (when NoSQL fits) and the Domain 3 conversion reconciliation items: tests where the old database's integrity rules land after a move to a document store. Public sources: COBIT 2019, DAMA-DMBOK.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a bank's database choice for fraud analysts tracing links among accounts, devices and payees, often many steps apart. Which model would the IS auditor expect as the BEST fit?

options.A: A relational database that joins tables on shared keys
options.B: A graph database that stores records as linked nodes
options.C: A key-value store that looks up each account by number
options.D: A hierarchical database that gives each record one parent

questions.key_concept: Choose the database model by the workload: graph stores suit many-step relationship queries, relational suits transactions, key-value suits simple lookups.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the workload mostly does with the data: look it up, total it, or follow links.
questions.correct_explanation: A graph database stores each account, device and payee as a node and each link as a stored relationship, so following a chain many steps deep is fast and direct. That fits fraud-ring analysis. A relational database is the runner-up: it can join tables on shared keys, but every extra step adds another join, so deep link queries grow slow and complex.

wrong_explanations.A: Relational joins work for a few steps, but each extra step adds another join, so deep link searches become slow and complex.
wrong_explanations.C: A key-value store finds one record by its key quickly but holds no relationships between records to follow.
wrong_explanations.D: A hierarchical model gives each record a single parent, so a device or payee shared by many accounts fits poorly.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because key-value stores hold no links between records and hierarchical trees allow only one parent per record.
Final two: B beats A because relational joins slow down with every extra step, while a graph stores the links themselves.
Exam cue: match the model to the workload; following relationships points to graph, totaling transactions to relational, simple lookups to key-value.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI03 (Managed Solutions Identification and Build); DAMA-DMBOK 2nd Edition (Data Modeling and Design, Data Storage and Operations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Database Models. Many-Step Relationship Queries'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A11.1 (Wave 3 coverage batch Q15: thin subtopic). Distinct from d4_055 (which workload supports choosing NoSQL in general) and d4_056 (legacy hierarchical database risks): tests matching a many-step relationship workload to the graph model. Public sources: COBIT 2019, DAMA-DMBOK.

questions.subtopic: Privileged Database Access. Evidence When Native Auditing Is Off
questions.question: An IS auditor learns that a database administrator (DBA) switched off native auditing before exporting customer records. Which source would MOST reliably show which records the DBA read?

options.A: The transaction log the database keeps for recovery
options.B: Query logs from a database activity monitoring agent or sensor
options.C: Firewall logs of the DBA's connections to the database server
options.D: A written account from the DBA, confirmed by the DBA's manager

questions.key_concept: DAM captures queries through its own agent or network sensor, so it stays reliable evidence when DBAs switch off native auditing.
questions.pre_read: Ask which source is independent of the DBA and also shows what was read, not just that a connection happened.
questions.correct_explanation: Database activity monitoring (DAM) captures each query through its own host agent or network sensor, apart from the database, so it keeps recording when native auditing is switched off. It is independent of the DBA and shows the records read. Firewall logs are the runner-up: they are independent too, but show only that the DBA connected, not which records were read.

wrong_explanations.A: Transaction logs record data changes for recovery, not reads, so they cannot show which records the DBA read.
wrong_explanations.C: Firewall logs show that the DBA connected to the server, not which queries ran or which records were read.
wrong_explanations.D: A written account is testimony from the person under review; a manager's confirmation does not make it independent evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because transaction logs hold changes, not reads, and the DBA's own account is testimony from the person under review.
Final two: B beats C because both are independent of the DBA, but only database activity monitoring records which queries ran, not just that a connection happened.
Exam cue: when the people under review can switch off a log, prefer evidence captured by a tool outside their control.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SI-4 (System Monitoring); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A.8.16 (Monitoring activities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Privileged Database Access. Evidence When Native Auditing Is Off'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A11.6 (batch Q16: practice for the web v12.24 study notes). Distinct from d4_156 (moving audit log administration away from DBAs) and d4_048 (tamper-resistant logging of DBA activity): tests which evidence source shows a DBA's reads when native auditing was switched off. Revised after the Q16 review (D4 auditor S3): rewritten from a mechanism question to an evidence-source choice. Public sources: ISACA ITAF, NIST and ISO.

questions.subtopic: Database Encryption. Choosing Fields for Further Encryption
questions.question: After an IS auditor reports that database administrators can read diagnosis fields protected only by transparent data encryption (TDE), the IT director asks the auditor to pick fields to encrypt. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Pick the fields using the data classification policy and document why
options.B: Let the database administrators choose the fields they do not need
options.C: Recommend that the data owner decide which fields need encryption
options.D: Advise that TDE already encrypts the whole database, so none are needed

questions.key_concept: The data owner decides which fields need encryption beyond TDE and accepts residual risk; the IS auditor recommends, not designs.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the decision being requested, and whether the IS auditor would later have to audit it.
questions.correct_explanation: Deciding which fields need protection beyond TDE is a control design and risk decision that belongs to the data owner, who also accepts any residual risk. The IS auditor recommends and later tests the result. Choosing fields from the classification policy is the runner-up: it sounds objective, but the IS auditor would then be designing the control it must later audit.

wrong_explanations.A: The classification policy would make the choice consistent, yet picking fields means designing the control; the data owner decides and the auditor recommends.
wrong_explanations.B: Administrators are the people the extra encryption must protect against, so letting them choose the fields defeats segregation of duties.
wrong_explanations.D: TDE decrypts data for anyone the database lets in, administrators included, so it does not address the reported finding.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because administrators cannot choose controls over themselves, and TDE shows clear text to anyone the database lets in.
Final two: C beats A because the IS auditor recommends while the data owner decides; picking the fields means designing the control.
Exam cue: when management asks the IS auditor to make a control decision, route it to the owner with a recommendation.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor Objectivity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A.8.24 (Use of cryptography)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Database Encryption. Choosing Fields for Further Encryption'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 4A11.6 (batch Q16: practice for the web v12.24 study notes). Distinct from d5_072 (which control stops administrators reading card numbers under TDE) and d3_071 (auditor asked to design application controls; same role lesson, different context): tests who decides the fields to encrypt and the IS auditor's role. Public sources: ISACA ITAF, NIST and ISO.

questions.subtopic: Operational Resilience. Testing a Provider Outage
questions.question: A bank's board asks whether the card payment service could keep running if its main cloud provider failed on its busiest shopping day. Which test should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: A failover test showing each system meets its recovery time objective
options.B: A review of the cloud provider's latest independent assurance report
options.C: A penetration test of the payment service's internet-facing systems
options.D: A scenario test of the whole service against its impact tolerance

questions.key_concept: Operational resilience tests ask whether a whole service stays within its impact tolerance; disaster recovery tests ask whether a system meets its recovery time objective.
questions.pre_read: Ask what question the test must answer: whether a part comes back, or whether the service keeps working.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's question is about a whole customer service in a severe but plausible event, so the test must run that scenario end to end, including the provider, and measure the outcome against the service's impact tolerance. A failover test is the runner-up: even run perfectly, it shows single systems restore within their recovery time objectives, not whether the service survives the provider's loss.

wrong_explanations.A: Failover tests prove components restore within their recovery time objectives; the service can still fail through provider, people or data dependencies they never touch.
wrong_explanations.B: An assurance report describes the provider's own controls; it cannot show whether this payment service keeps running when the provider fails.
wrong_explanations.C: A penetration test looks for security weaknesses, not whether the service keeps running through a major supplier outage.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because an assurance report covers the provider's controls and a penetration test looks for security weaknesses, not continuity.
Final two: D beats A because a failover test answers a different question: whether parts restore, not whether the service survives.
Exam cue: match the test to the question asked; service survival needs a service-level scenario test, not component recovery tests.

questions.subtopic: Impact Tolerances. Handling a Tolerance Breach
questions.question: A resilience exercise shows the online claims service would be down five days in a regional outage, against a two-day impact tolerance, and the fix exceeds budget. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Senior management approves and funds a dated plan to close the gap
options.B: The claims service owner postpones the fix until next year's budget
options.C: The IT team raises the tolerance to five days to match recovery
options.D: Senior management funds the cheapest recovery fixes this year

questions.key_concept: Senior management sets impact tolerances and decides each breach: it approves and funds a dated plan that brings the service back within tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Ask who set the limit that was breached, and who can therefore approve the spending to close the gap.
questions.correct_explanation: Senior management sets impact tolerances, so a breach that needs unbudgeted money goes back to it first: it approves and funds a dated plan that brings the service back within tolerance. The service owner deferring the fix is the runner-up: the owner tracks remediation, but cannot alone leave a service outside a tolerance senior management set, especially when the fix needs budget.

wrong_explanations.B: The service owner tracks the fix but cannot alone defer a breach of a tolerance that senior management set and must fund.
wrong_explanations.C: Tolerances reflect the harm customers can bear, not what recovery can achieve; raising one to match results hides the gap instead of closing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Funding just the cheapest fixes leaves the service outside tolerance with no dated plan to close the gap; the fix must match the tolerance, not the lowest cost.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because raising the tolerance to match recovery defeats its purpose, and funding the cheapest fixes leaves the service outside tolerance with no plan to close the gap.
Final two: A beats B because only senior management, which set the tolerance, can fund the fix; the service owner cannot defer a breach alone.
Exam cue: when a gap needs money or exceeds an approved limit, the decision goes to whoever set the limit: fund a dated fix or formally accept the gap.

questions.question: A bank sends every card payment to one external fraud-scoring provider with no alternate, and the service has brief outages most months. Which risk should the IS auditor rate as GREATEST?

options.A: Recurring outages delay card payment approvals most months
options.B: Fraud scores are slightly less accurate than an in-house model
options.C: The bank cannot audit a service that it does not run
options.D: A lasting provider failure leaves no way to score payments

questions.key_concept: With one supplier and no alternate, the greatest risk is losing that supplier; brief outages are more frequent, but their impact is bounded.
questions.pre_read: Weigh how likely each event is and how much harm it would do, noting the bank has no alternate provider.
questions.correct_explanation: With no alternate, a lasting provider failure would leave the bank unable to screen card payments: it must stop payments or accept unscreened fraud until a replacement is found. Monthly brief outages are the runner-up. They are more likely, but each delay is short and recoverable, so their impact is bounded, while the concentration risk is not.

wrong_explanations.A: Recurring outages are the most likely event and do disrupt payments, but each is short and recoverable; losing the only provider would halt payment screening outright.
wrong_explanations.B: A small accuracy gap has limited impact compared with losing fraud screening entirely, and nothing in the stem suggests the scores are poor.
wrong_explanations.C: Outsourcing does not remove audit access; the bank can use contract audit rights and the provider's independent assurance reports.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because a slight accuracy gap is minor, and contract rights and assurance reports let the bank audit an outsourced service.
Final two: D beats A because, with no alternate, losing the provider would halt payment screening outright, while each brief outage is short and recoverable.
Exam cue: GREATEST weighs likelihood with impact; a realistic event with severe, open-ended harm outranks frequent small, bounded ones, but a remote catastrophe does not outrank a likely severe risk.

questions.subtopic: Business Impact Analysis. From Draft to Approval
questions.question: A continuity team has drafted a business impact analysis (BIA) from process owners' questionnaire answers and plans to present it to senior management next week. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Senior management approves the draft impact results and recovery priorities
options.B: The continuity team checks ratings against records and agreed criteria
options.C: IT sets recovery time objectives from current recovery capability
options.D: The continuity team selects recovery strategies for the top tier

questions.key_concept: BIA data from questionnaires is validated against records and ranked on common criteria before senior management approves it.
questions.pre_read: Ask which plausible step needs another step's output before it can be done soundly.
questions.correct_explanation: Questionnaire answers are self-reported, so the draft ratings are first checked against records, such as revenue and transaction volumes, and ranked on one set of impact criteria. Senior management approval is the runner-up. It is essential before strategies are chosen, but approving unvalidated ratings would lock in priorities that may be inflated or wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval is required, but it should rest on validated ratings; approving self-reported answers first locks in priorities that may be inflated or wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Recovery targets come from business impact, not from what IT can recover today; starting from current capability hides the gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Strategies are chosen only after the BIA is validated and approved; selecting them now builds on an unagreed basis.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because recovery targets come from business impact, not IT capability, and strategies follow an approved BIA.
Final two: B beats A because approval is only as sound as the ratings it accepts; validate them first, then seek approval.
Exam cue: an approval is only as sound as what it approves; when approving and validating the input both look right, validate first.
